questions.question:
Given a 6×6 2D array `arr`, an *hourglass* is a subset of values with indices falling in this pattern within the array:

```
a b c
  d
e f g
```

There are **16** hourglasses in the array. Calculate the hourglass sum for every hourglass, then return the **maximum** hourglass sum.

An hourglass sum may be negative — at least one hourglass always exists.
questions.title: 2D Array - DS

questions.question:
Given an integer array `nums`, return all the triplets `[nums[i], nums[j], nums[k]]` such that `i != j`, `i != k`, and `j != k`, and `nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] == 0`.

Notice that the solution set must **not contain duplicate triplets**.
questions.title: 3Sum

questions.question: Start with a 1-indexed array of `n` zeros. You're given `m` operations; each is a triple `[a, b, k]` meaning *add `k` to every element from index `a` to index `b` inclusive*. After performing all `m` operations, return the **maximum value** in the array.
questions.title: Array Manipulation

questions.question:
Given an array `a` of `n` integers, print or return the elements in **reverse** order. If the input is `1 4 3 2`, the reversed array is `2 3 4 1`.

Implement the reversal yourself; do the work in place where possible.
questions.title: Arrays: DS (Reverse an Array)
constraints: The array may have a single element
Reverse in place is preferred (O(1) extra space)

questions.question:
A left rotation operation on an array shifts each of the array's elements `1` unit to the left. For example, if `2` left rotations are performed on array `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`, the array becomes `[3, 4, 5, 1, 2]`.

Given an array `a` of `n` integers and a number `d`, perform `d` left rotations on the array and return the resulting array.
questions.title: Arrays: Left Rotation

questions.question:
You are given an integer array `prices` where `prices[i]` is the price of a given stock on the `i`-th day.

On each day, you may decide to buy and/or sell the stock. You can only hold **at most one** share of the stock at any time. However, you can buy it then immediately sell it on the **same day**.

Find and return the **maximum profit** you can achieve.
questions.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II

questions.question:
You are given an array `prices` where `prices[i]` is the price of a given stock on the `iᵗʰ` day.

You want to maximize your profit by choosing a **single day to buy** one stock and choosing a **different day in the future to sell** that stock.

Return the maximum profit you can achieve from this transaction. If you cannot achieve any profit, return `0`.
questions.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock

questions.question:
Anna and Brian are sharing a meal and splitting the bill, but Brian forgot that Anna did not eat item `k`. The cost of each item is given in an array `bill`.

Anna's fair share is half the cost of everything **except** item `k`. Brian charged Anna `b`.

If `b` equals Anna's fair share, print `"Bon Appetit"`. Otherwise, Anna was overcharged — print the difference `b − fairShare`, the amount Brian owes her back.
questions.title: Bill Division (Bon Appétit)
constraints: 0 ≤ k < n (index of the item Anna did not eat)
total − bill[k] is even, so the split is exact
b is the amount Anna was actually charged

questions.title: Sorting: Bubble Sort
constraints: 1 ≤ a[i] ≤ 2·10⁹ (values can be large; comparisons only)
The array may already be sorted (0 swaps) or reverse sorted (n(n−1)/2 swaps)
The swap count can reach ~5×10⁹, beyond 32-bit int

questions.question:
There are `n` children standing in a line, each assigned a rating value given in the integer array `ratings`.

You are giving candies to these children subject to the following requirements:

- Each child must have **at least one** candy.
- Children with a higher rating get **more** candies than their neighbors.

Return the **minimum** number of candies you need to have to distribute the candies to the children.
questions.title: Candy

questions.question:
Given a list of unsorted integers `arr`, find the pair(s) of elements that have the smallest absolute difference between them.

If there are multiple pairs tied for the smallest difference, list them all. Each pair must be printed with the smaller element first, and the pairs themselves listed in ascending order.
questions.title: Closest Numbers
constraints: All differences fit comfortably in a 32-bit int (max gap ≤ 2·10⁷)
At least one pair always exists since n ≥ 2

questions.question:
You are given an integer array `height` of length `n`. There are `n` vertical lines drawn such that the two endpoints of the `iᵗʰ` line are `(i, 0)` and `(i, height[i])`.

Find two lines that together with the x-axis form a container, such that the container contains the **most water**. Return the maximum amount of water a container can store.

Notice that you may not slant the container.
questions.title: Container With Most Water

questions.question: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return `true` if there are two ***distinct indices*** `i` and `j` in the array such that `nums[i] == nums[j]` and `abs(i - j) <= k`.
questions.title: Contains Duplicate II

questions.question: Given an integer array `nums`, return `true` if any value appears **at least twice** in the array, and return `false` if every element is distinct.
questions.title: Contains Duplicate

questions.question:
Given an array `nums`, count the number of **inversions** — pairs of indices `(i, j)` such that `i < j` and `nums[i] > nums[j]`.

Inversions measure how far the array is from sorted: a sorted array has `0`, a reverse-sorted array has the maximum `n(n−1)/2`.
questions.title: Count Inversions
constraints: The answer can reach ~5 × 10⁹ — return a 64-bit integer

questions.question:
Given an array `arr` of `n` integers and an integer `target`, count the number of pairs of indices `(i, j)` with `i < j` such that `arr[i] + arr[j] = target`.

Return the count. Values may repeat and may be negative.
questions.title: Count Pairs with given sum
constraints: Pairs are unordered: (i, j) and (j, i) are the same pair

questions.question:
You are given an array `arr` of `n` integers and a positive integer `r`. A triplet `(arr[i], arr[j], arr[k])` is a geometric progression with ratio `r` if `i < j < k` and `arr[j] = arr[i]·r` and `arr[k] = arr[j]·r`.

Return the **number of such index triplets**. Because values can repeat, two triplets are different if any of their indices differ.
questions.title: Count Triplets
constraints: The answer can exceed 32-bit range — use 64-bit (long)

questions.question:
Given a list of integers, count the number of times each value appears. All values are in the range `0` to `99` inclusive.

Return an array `result` of length `100` where `result[i]` is the number of times the value `i` occurs in the input.
questions.title: Counting Sort 1
constraints: Output is always a list of exactly 100 counts

questions.question: Given a list of integers in the range `0` to `99`, return the list sorted in non-decreasing order **using counting sort** (no comparison-based sort).
questions.title: Counting Sort 2
constraints: Output is the input sorted in non-decreasing order

questions.question: Given an array of integers `a` and a positive integer `k`, count the number of `(i, j)` pairs where `i < j` and `(a[i] + a[j])` is **divisible by** `k`.
questions.title: Divisible Sum Pairs

questions.question:
Declare `n` empty sequences and a variable `lastAnswer = 0`. Process `q` queries; each query has a type and two integers `x` and `y`.

For every query, compute `idx = (x XOR lastAnswer) % n`.

- **Type 1** `1 x y`: append integer `y` to the sequence at index `idx`.
- **Type 2** `2 x y`: assign `lastAnswer = seq[idx][y % size(seq[idx])]` and record `lastAnswer`.

Return the list of all values recorded by type-2 queries, in order.
questions.title: Dynamic Array
constraints: Each type-2 query targets a sequence with at least one element

questions.question:
Given an array `nums`, find an **equilibrium index** — an index `i` where the sum of all elements at positions `< i` equals the sum of all elements at positions `> i`.

Return the leftmost such index, or `-1` if none exists. The element at `i` is excluded from both sides.
questions.title: Equilibrium Index
constraints: An empty side counts as sum 0

questions.question:
Given an array `nums` of `n + 1` integers where each value is in the range `[1, n]`, there is exactly one repeated number. Return that repeated number.

You must **not modify** the array and must use only **constant** extra space, in better than O(n²) time.
questions.title: Find the Duplicate Number
constraints: 1 ≤ nums[i] ≤ n (every value is a valid index into nums)
Exactly one value is duplicated; it may appear more than twice

questions.question:
HackerLand National Bank flags potentially fraudulent account activity. A client gets a notification if their **spending on a given day is greater than or equal to 2× the median** of their expenditures over the **trailing `d` days**.

Given the number of trailing days `d` and an array `expenditure` of daily spends, determine how many notifications the client receives over a period of `n` days. The client must have at least `d` prior days of data before any notification can be sent.
questions.title: Fraudulent Activity Notifications
constraints: 0 ≤ expenditure[i] ≤ 200  (bounded — this is the key to counting sort)
Notifications can only start from day index d (0-based)

questions.question:
Process a sequence of queries, each of one of three types:

- `1 x` — **insert** the value `x` into the data structure.
- `2 x` — **delete** one occurrence of `x` (do nothing if `x` is not present).
- `3 x` — **check** whether any integer currently appears exactly `x` times; output `1` if so, `0` otherwise.

Return the list of answers, one per type-3 query, in order.
questions.title: Frequency Queries
constraints: Deleting an absent value is a no-op
Type-3 x is a frequency to test (x ≥ 1 in practice)

questions.question:
Gridland has a network of train tracks on an `n × m` grid. There are `k` tracks; track `i` is described by three integers `r, c1, c2` meaning row `r` has a track spanning columns `c1` through `c2` (inclusive). The city wants to build lampposts on every cell that has **no** train track.

Given `n`, `m`, and the `k` tracks, determine the number of cells where a lamppost can be placed.
questions.title: Gridland Metro
constraints: 1 ≤ r ≤ n, and 1 ≤ c1 ≤ c2 ≤ m

questions.question:
Given an array of integers `citations` where `citations[i]` is the number of citations a researcher received for their `i`-th paper, return the researcher's **h-index**.

The h-index is defined as the maximum value of `h` such that the given researcher has published at least `h` papers that have each been cited at least `h` times.
questions.title: H-Index

questions.question:
Each time Sunny and Johnny take a trip to the Ice Cream Parlor, they pool their money. Given the amount `money` they have and a list of flavor `cost`s (where the id of a flavor is its **1-based** position in the list), determine the ids of the two distinct flavors they can purchase such that the costs sum to exactly `money`.

Return the two ids in increasing order. There is exactly one solution per trip.
questions.title: Hash Tables: Ice Cream Parlor
constraints: 1 ≤ cost[i] ≤ 10⁴, and exactly one valid pair exists

questions.question:
On a trip to the Ice Cream Parlor, you have a fixed amount of `money` and a list of flavor `cost`s. A flavor's id is its **1-based** index in the list. Choose two distinct flavors whose costs sum to exactly `money` and return their ids in increasing order.

Exactly one valid pair exists for each trip.
questions.title: Ice Cream Parlor
constraints: 1 ≤ cost[i] ≤ 10⁴, with exactly one valid pair

questions.question:
Implement the `RandomizedSet` class:

- `RandomizedSet()` initializes the `RandomizedSet` object.
- `bool insert(int val)` inserts an item `val` into the set if not present. Returns `true` if the item was not present, `false` otherwise.
- `bool remove(int val)` removes an item `val` from the set if present. Returns `true` if the item was present, `false` otherwise.
- `int getRandom()` returns a random element from the current set of elements (it's guaranteed that at least one element exists when this method is called). ***Each element must have the same probability of being returned.***

You must implement the functions of the class such that each function works in ***average O(1) time complexity***.
questions.title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)

examples.input: insert(1), remove(2), insert(2), getRandom(), remove(1), insert(2), getRandom()
examples.output: true, false, true, [1 or 2], true, false, 2

examples.input: insert(0), insert(1), remove(0), insert(2), remove(1), getRandom()

constraints: At most 2 × 10⁵ calls will be made to insert, remove, and getRandom
There will be at least one element in the data structure when getRandom is called

questions.question:
There is a game where you start at cloud `0` and want to reach the last cloud. The clouds are given as an array `c` where `c[i] = 0` is a *cumulus* cloud (safe to land on) and `c[i] = 1` is a *thundercloud* (cannot be landed on).

From any cloud `i` you may jump to cloud `i + 1` or cloud `i + 2`, as long as the cloud you land on is safe. Each jump counts as one move. Determine the **minimum number of jumps** required to reach the last cloud. It is guaranteed that a path exists and the first and last clouds are safe.
questions.title: Jumping on the Clouds
constraints: c[0] = 0 and c[n − 1] = 0 (start and end are always safe)
There are never two adjacent thunderclouds, so a path always exists

questions.question:
Given an unsorted array of integers `nums`, return the length of the longest consecutive elements sequence.

You must write an algorithm that runs in **O(n)** time.
questions.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence

questions.question:
Given an array `nums` of size `n`, return *the majority element*.

The majority element is the element that appears **more than** `⌊n / 2⌋` times. You may assume that the majority element ***always exists*** in the array.
questions.title: Majority Element
constraints: A majority element is guaranteed to exist

questions.question:
Given an `n × n` grid of integers, an *hourglass* is the set of 7 cells in this shape anchored at a top-left corner `(r, c)`:

```
a b c
  d
e f g
```

Compute the hourglass sum for every position where the shape fits inside the grid, and return the **maximum** hourglass sum. Sums may be negative.
questions.title: Maximum Hourglass Sum

questions.question:
Given an array of `n` elements and a modulo `m`, find the maximum value of `(sum of elements of a subarray) mod m`, taken over all **non-empty contiguous** subarrays.

In other words, maximize `(a[l] + a[l+1] + … + a[r]) mod m` over all `0 ≤ l ≤ r < n`.
questions.title: Maximum Subarray Sum
constraints: The answer is a value in the range [0, m − 1]

questions.question:
Given an integer array `nums`, find the ***contiguous*** subarray (containing at least one number) which has the **largest sum**, and return its sum.

A **subarray** is a contiguous part of an array.
questions.title: Maximum Subarray (Kadane's)
constraints: The subarray must contain at least one element
Elements may be negative, zero, or positive

questions.question:
Given an array `nums` of integers, count the number of **inversions**: pairs of indices `(i, j)` such that `i < j` and `nums[i] > nums[j]`.

The inversion count measures how far the array is from being sorted in ascending order — a sorted array has 0 inversions, a strictly descending array has the maximum `n(n−1)/2`.
questions.title: Count Inversions in an Array
constraints: The answer can be as large as n(n−1)/2 ≈ 5 × 10⁹ — use a 64-bit integer
Equal values do NOT form an inversion (strict >)

questions.question:
An inversion in an array is a pair of indices `(i, j)` such that `i < j` and `arr[i] > arr[j]`. This is exactly the number of swaps a bubble/insertion sort would perform to sort the array.

For each query array, return the total number of inversions.

Because the count can be large, return it as a 64-bit integer (`long`).
questions.title: Merge Sort: Counting Inversions
constraints: Answer can be as large as n(n−1)/2 ≈ 5·10⁹ — requires a 64-bit integer

questions.question:
You are given two integer arrays `nums1` and `nums2`, sorted in **non-decreasing order**, and two integers `m` and `n` representing the number of elements in `nums1` and `nums2` respectively.

**Merge** `nums1` and `nums2` into a single array sorted in non-decreasing order.

The final sorted array should **not** be returned by the function, but instead be *stored inside the array* `nums1`. To accommodate this, `nums1` has a length of `m + n`, where the first `m` elements are the ones that should be merged, and the last `n` elements are set to `0` and should be ignored. `nums2` has a length of `n`.
questions.title: Merge Sorted Array

questions.question: There are five types of migratory birds, identified by ids `1` through `5`. Given an array `arr` where each element is the type id of a bird sighted, return the id of the bird type that was sighted **the most**. If more than one type shares the maximum count, return the **smallest** such id.
questions.title: Migratory Birds
constraints: It is guaranteed at least one bird of some type is sighted

questions.question:
Given an array of integers `arr`, find the **minimum absolute difference** between any two elements in the array.

The absolute difference of two elements `a` and `b` is `|a − b|`. Return the smallest such value over all pairs.
questions.title: Minimum Absolute Difference in an Array
constraints: Elements may be negative and may repeat
There are at least two elements, so a pair always exists

questions.question:
Lauren has a chart of the price of a particular house over the years. Each year she could buy the house and, in some **later** year, sell it. She is only interested in transactions that result in a **loss** — selling for strictly less than she paid.

Given the prices indexed by year, find the **minimum loss** Lauren can incur. It is guaranteed that at least one losing transaction is possible, and all prices are distinct.
questions.title: Minimum Loss
constraints: At least one valid (buy earlier, sell later at a loss) transaction exists

questions.question:
Given an array of **positive** integers `nums` and a positive integer `target`, return the **minimal length** of a contiguous subarray of which the sum is **greater than or equal to** `target`.

If there is no such subarray, return `0` instead.

Follow-up: if you have figured out the O(n) solution, try coding another solution of which the time complexity is O(n log n).
questions.title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum

questions.question: You are given an unordered array consisting of consecutive integers `[1, 2, 3, …, n]` without any duplicates. You are allowed to swap **any two elements** (not just adjacent ones). Find and return the **minimum number of swaps** required to sort the array in ascending order.
questions.title: Minimum Swaps 2
constraints: The array is a permutation of the integers 1..n (each appears exactly once)
Swaps may be between any two positions, not only adjacent ones

questions.question:
Given two arrays of integers, find which elements of the **original** array are missing from the **reduced** array. Numbers may occur **multiple times**; a number is missing as many times as the original has more copies than the reduced one.

Return the **distinct** missing numbers in **ascending** order. It is guaranteed every value in the reduced array also appears in the original, and the range of values satisfies `max − min ≤ 100`.
questions.title: Missing Numbers
constraints: 1 ≤ n, m ≤ 2 × 10⁵ (sizes of reduced and original arrays)
Every reduced element appears in the original

questions.question:
Given an integer array `nums`, move all `0`'s to the **end** of it while maintaining the *relative order* of the non-zero elements.

**Note** that you must do this *in place* without making a copy of the array.
questions.title: Move Zeroes

questions.question:
Initially, people are standing in a queue numbered `1` to `n` in order. Any person can bribe the person directly in front of them to swap positions, but **each person can bribe at most twice**.

Given the final state of the queue `q`, determine the **minimum number of bribes** that took place to reach it. If anyone has bribed more than twice — detectable because their label has moved more than 2 positions forward — print `Too chaotic` instead.
questions.title: New Year Chaos
constraints: Each person bribes at most twice when the state is valid

questions.question:
Given an array of integers, find the longest subarray where the absolute difference between any two elements is **less than or equal to 1**.

Note: subsequences (any order, not necessarily contiguous) are allowed — you are choosing the largest group of elements, not a contiguous run. Return the **size** of that group.
questions.title: Picking Numbers
constraints: The result is at least 1 (any single element trivially satisfies the condition)

questions.question:
Given an integer array `nums`, return an array `answer` such that `answer[i]` is equal to the **product of all the elements of `nums` except `nums[i]`**.

The product of any prefix or suffix of `nums` is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit integer. You must write an algorithm that runs in **O(n)** time and **without using the division operation**.
questions.title: Product of Array Except Self
constraints: The product of any prefix or suffix fits in a 32-bit integer
Follow-up: O(1) extra space (the output array does not count)

questions.question:
Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the **kth largest** element in the array.

Note that it is the kth largest element in sorted order, **not** the kth distinct element — duplicates count toward the rank.

Can you solve it without fully sorting the array?
questions.title: Kth Largest Element via Quickselect
constraints: Duplicates are allowed and count toward the rank

questions.question:
Given an array `arr`, partition it around the first element `p = arr[0]` (the pivot).

Reorder the array so that all elements less than `p` come before `p`, and all elements greater than `p` come after it. You do not need to sort the array — just produce a valid partition.

Return the partitioned array.
questions.title: Quicksort 1 - Partition
constraints: All elements are distinct (so no element equals the pivot besides the pivot itself)

questions.question:
Using the partition logic from Quicksort 1, implement a recursive quicksort that fully sorts the array.

The pivot for each sub-array is its first element. After sorting a sub-array (combining its sorted left part, the pivot, and its sorted right part), print that sub-array — but only when it has more than one element.

The final line printed is the fully sorted array.
questions.title: Quicksort 2 - Sorting (Partition)
constraints: Elements are distinct in the challenge inputs
Pivot is always the first element of the current sub-array

questions.question:
Given an integer array `nums` sorted in **non-decreasing order**, remove some duplicates **in-place** such that each unique element appears **at most twice**. The relative order of the elements should be kept the same.

Since it is impossible to change the length of the array in some languages, you must instead have the result be placed in the first part of the array `nums`. More formally, if there are `k` elements after removing the duplicates, then the first `k` elements of `nums` should hold the final result. It does not matter what you leave beyond the first `k` elements.

Return `k` after placing the final result in the first `k` slots of `nums`.
questions.title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array II
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order

questions.question:
Given an integer array `nums` sorted in **non-decreasing order**, remove the duplicates *in place* such that each unique element appears only **once**. The *relative order* of the elements should be kept the same. Then return the number of unique elements in `nums`.

Consider the number of unique elements of `nums` to be `k`. To get accepted, you need to do the following:

- Change the array `nums` such that the first `k` elements of `nums` contain the unique elements in the order they were present initially. The remaining elements of `nums` are not important as well as the size of `nums`.
- Return `k`.
questions.title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order

questions.question:
Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `val`, remove all occurrences of `val` in `nums` **in-place**. The order of the elements may be changed. Then return the number of elements in `nums` which are not equal to `val`.

Consider the number of elements in `nums` which are not equal to `val` to be `k` — to get accepted, you need to do the following:

- Change the array `nums` such that the first `k` elements of `nums` contain the elements which are not equal to `val`. The remaining elements of `nums` are not important.
- Return `k`.
questions.title: Remove Element

questions.question:
Given an integer array `nums`, rotate the array to the right by `k` steps, where `k` is non-negative.

Do it **in-place** with `O(1)` extra space if you can — that's the follow-up the interviewer cares about.
questions.title: Rotate Array

questions.question:
Watson gives Sherlock an array of integers. He asks whether there exists an index such that the sum of the elements to the **left** of that index equals the sum of the elements to the **right** of that index.

For each query, print `YES` if such an index exists, otherwise print `NO`. The element at the chosen index is counted on neither side.
questions.title: Sherlock and Array
constraints: There may be more than one valid index; you only need to know if at least one exists

questions.question:
There is a large pile of socks that must be paired by color. Given an array of integers `ar` representing the color of each sock, determine **how many pairs of socks** with matching colors there are.

A pair consists of two socks of the *same* color. Return the total number of complete matching pairs.
questions.title: Sock Merchant

questions.question:
Given an integer array `nums` sorted in **non-decreasing** order, return an array of **the squares of each number** sorted in non-decreasing order.

Follow-up: can you do it in O(n) time using a two-pointer technique, rather than the straightforward O(n log n) of squaring then sorting?
questions.title: Squares of a Sorted Array
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order

questions.question:
The span of a stock's price on day `i` is the maximum number of consecutive days (ending on day `i`, counting day `i`) for which the price was less than or equal to the price on day `i`.

Given the daily prices, return the span for each day. In the streaming version, return each span as its price arrives.
questions.title: Stock Span
constraints: Span values are in [1, i + 1] for day i

questions.question:
Lily has a chocolate bar represented by an array `s`, where `s[i]` is the number of squares in the i-th piece. Ron's birthday is on month `m` and day `d`.

Lily wants to break off a **contiguous** segment of the bar that contains exactly `m` squares-pieces and whose squares **sum to** `d`.

Given `s`, `d`, and `m`, return the **number of ways** to choose such a contiguous segment of length `m` whose values add up to `d`.
questions.title: Subarray Division (Lily's Chocolate)
constraints: Segments are contiguous and may overlap

questions.question:
You are given `n` items, each a pair `(x, s)` where `x` is an integer key in `0..99` and `s` is a string. Two transformations and a sort:

1. For the first half of the items (those with original 0-based index `i < n/2`), replace the string `s` with a single dash `'-'`.
2. Stably sort all items by their integer key `x`.
3. Print the resulting strings in order, separated by single spaces.

Stability means items sharing a key must appear in their original input order.
questions.title: The Full Counting Sort

examples.input:
n = 20
0 ab
6 cd
0 ef
6 gh
4 ij
0 ab
6 cd
0 ef
6 gh
0 ij
4 that
3 be
0 to
1 be
5 question
1 or
2 not
4 is
2 to
4 the
examples.output: - - - - - to be or not to be - that is the question - - - -

constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁶ (n is even in the standard input)
Sort must be stable on the key x

questions.question: Given `n` non-negative integers representing an elevation map where the width of each bar is 1, compute how much water it can trap after raining.
questions.title: Trapping Rain Water

questions.question:
You are given three arrays of integers `a`, `b`, and `c` of sizes `p`, `q`, and `r` respectively. Count the number of **distinct triplets** `(x, y, z)` where `x` is an element of `a`, `y` is an element of `b`, `z` is an element of `c`, satisfying both `x ≤ y` and `z ≤ y`.

Two triplets are the same if all three values are equal, so duplicate values within an array should be treated as one.
questions.title: Triple Sum
constraints: The answer can exceed the 32-bit integer range
Values may repeat within an array but distinct triplets are counted once

questions.question:
Given a **1-indexed** array of integers `numbers` that is already sorted in non-decreasing order, find two numbers such that they add up to a specific `target`.

Return the indices of the two numbers, `index1` and `index2`, **added by one** as an integer array `[index1, index2]` of length 2, where `1 ≤ index1 < index2 ≤ numbers.length`.

The tests are generated such that there is ***exactly one solution***. You may not use the same element twice. Your solution must use only **constant extra space**.
questions.title: Two Sum II — Input Array Is Sorted
constraints: numbers is sorted in non-decreasing order

questions.question:
Given an array of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return **the indices** of the two numbers such that they add up to `target`.

You may assume that each input would have ***exactly one solution***, and you may not use the same element twice.

You can return the answer in any order.
questions.title: Two Sum

questions.question:
Determine if a 9×9 Sudoku board is valid. Only the **filled cells** need to be validated according to the following rules:

1. Each row must contain the digits 1–9 without repetition.
2. Each column must contain the digits 1–9 without repetition.
3. Each of the nine 3×3 sub-boxes must contain the digits 1–9 without repetition.

The board may be partially filled, where empty cells are denoted by '.'. A partially filled board that does not violate any rule is still **valid**.
questions.title: Valid Sudoku

examples.input: A standard partially-filled board with no repeats
Same board but with two 8s in the top-left box

constraints: Only the filled cells are validated

questions.question:
Given an array of **distinct** integers `candidates` and a target integer `target`, return a list of **all unique combinations** of `candidates` where the chosen numbers sum to `target`.

The **same number may be chosen from `candidates` an unlimited number of times**. Two combinations are unique if the frequency of at least one of the chosen numbers is different.

The test cases are generated such that the number of unique combinations that sum up to `target` is less than 150 for the given input.
questions.title: Combination Sum
constraints: All elements of candidates are distinct

questions.question:
You are given a **10×10** crossword grid as 10 strings of length 10. A `+` denotes a blocked cell; a `-` denotes a blank to be filled. You are also given a single string of words separated by `;` (e.g. `"LONDON;DELHI;ICELAND;ANKARA"`).

Fill every blank so that each word from the list is placed exactly once, either left-to-right (horizontal) or top-to-bottom (vertical), occupying a maximal run of blanks. Where words cross, the shared cell must agree.

Return the solved grid as 10 strings. A unique solution is guaranteed.
questions.title: Crossword Puzzle

examples.input: grid with two crossing slots, words = ICELAND;MEXICO
examples.output: MEXICO horizontal and ICELAND vertical crossing at the shared 'I'/'C'

constraints: The number of words equals the number of slots (each word used exactly once)
Every slot is a maximal run of blanks of length ≥ 2
A unique solution is guaranteed to exist

questions.question:
Given an `n × n` chessboard, a **knight's tour** is a sequence of moves by a knight (an 'L'-shaped move) that visits every square exactly once. The knight starts at a given cell `(sr, sc)`.

Find a knight's tour if one exists — return the board labeled with visit order `0 .. n²-1` — and, in the counting variant, return the number of distinct open tours from the start cell.
questions.title: Knight's Tour (Count / Locate)

examples.output: a valid 5×5 open tour exists (board labeled 0..24)

constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 8 for exhaustive counting; finding one tour with Warnsdorff scales to larger n
A knight has up to 8 moves: (±1, ±2) and (±2, ±1)
Each cell must be visited exactly once (a Hamiltonian path on the knight-move graph)
For n < 5 (except trivial 1×1) no open tour exists on some boards — handle 'no tour' gracefully

questions.question:
Given a string containing digits from `2-9` inclusive, return **all possible letter combinations** that the number could represent. Return the answer in **any order**.

A mapping of digits to letters (just like on the telephone buttons) is given below. Note that **1 does not map to any letters**.

2→abc, 3→def, 4→ghi, 5→jkl, 6→mno, 7→pqrs, 8→tuv, 9→wxyz
questions.title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
constraints: digits[i] is a digit in the range ['2', '9']

questions.question:
The **n-queens** puzzle is the problem of placing `n` queens on an `n × n` chessboard such that **no two queens attack each other**.

Given an integer `n`, return **all distinct solutions** to the n-queens puzzle. You may return the answer in any order.

Each solution contains a distinct board configuration of the n-queens' placement, where `'Q'` and `'.'` indicate a queen and an empty space, respectively.
questions.title: N-Queens

questions.question:
Given a string `s`, partition `s` such that **every substring of the partition is a palindrome**. Return **all possible palindrome partitionings** of `s`.

A **palindrome** is a string that reads the same forward and backward.
questions.title: Palindrome Partitioning
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters

questions.question: Given an array `nums` of **distinct** integers, return **all the possible permutations**. You can return the answer in **any order**.
questions.title: Permutations
constraints: All the integers of nums are unique

questions.question:
You are given an `R × C` grid `maze` of 0s and 1s, where `1` is an open cell and `0` is a wall. A rat starts at the top-left cell `(0, 0)` and wants to reach the bottom-right cell `(R - 1, C - 1)`, moving one step at a time to an adjacent open cell.

Allowed moves are Down, Left, Right, and Up (the rat may not revisit a cell on its current path).

Return whether a path exists (and, in the all-paths variant, list every distinct path as a string of move letters). If the start or goal is a wall, no path exists.
questions.title: Rat in a Maze
constraints: The rat cannot step on a 0 cell or leave the grid
A cell cannot be revisited within the same path

questions.question:
Given a string `s`, generate **all permutations** of its characters and return them in **lexicographically sorted (dictionary) order**.

If the string contains repeated characters, each *distinct* permutation must appear exactly once.

For example, `s = "ab"` returns `["ab", "ba"]`, and `s = "aba"` returns `["aab", "aba", "baa"]`.
questions.title: Permutations of Strings
constraints: s consists of printable characters (commonly lowercase letters)
The string may contain repeated characters
Output must be in lexicographic order with no duplicate permutations
Number of distinct permutations ≤ n! (fewer when characters repeat)

questions.question:
Given an integer array `nums` of **unique** elements, return **all possible subsets** (the power set).

The solution set **must not contain duplicate subsets**. Return the solution in any order.
questions.title: Subsets
constraints: All the numbers of nums are unique

questions.question:
Find the number of ways that a given integer **X** can be expressed as the sum of the **N-th powers of unique, natural numbers**.

For example, if `X = 13` and `N = 2`, we have to find the number of ways to express 13 as a sum of squares of unique naturals: `13 = 2² + 3²` is the only way, so the answer is **1**.

Return the count of such representations.
questions.title: The Power Sum
constraints: Naturals used must be unique (each appears at most once)
Order does not matter — {1²,2²} and {2²,1²} are the same representation
The answer is a non-negative integer (0 if no representation exists)

questions.question:
You have three pegs — a **source**, an **auxiliary**, and a **target** — and `n` disks of distinct sizes stacked on the source peg in decreasing size (largest at the bottom).

Move all `n` disks to the target peg under two rules: move only one disk at a time (always the top disk of a peg), and never place a larger disk on top of a smaller one.

Print each move as `Move disk k from X to Y`, and return the total number of moves made.
questions.title: Tower of Hanoi

examples.output: Move disk 1 from A to C  (1 move)
disk 1 A→B, disk 2 A→C, disk 1 B→C  (3 moves)

constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 20 (so the move count 2ⁿ - 1 stays printable)
Disks start sorted largest-on-bottom on the source peg
The minimum number of moves is 2ⁿ - 1

questions.question:

The word can be constructed from letters of **sequentially adjacent cells**, where adjacent cells are horizontally or vertically neighboring. **The same letter cell may not be used more than once.**
questions.title: Word Search
constraints: board and word consist of only lowercase and uppercase English letters

questions.question:
You are given an array `stalls` of `n` integers, where `stalls[i]` is the position of the i-th stall on a number line, and an integer `c` — the number of cows.

The cows are aggressive, so you want to assign them to stalls such that the **minimum distance between any two cows is as large as possible**.

Return that largest possible minimum distance.
questions.title: Aggressive Cows
constraints: It is always possible to place all c cows

questions.question:
You are given an array `books` of `n` integers where `books[i]` is the number of pages in the i-th book, and an integer `k` — the number of students.

Allocate **all** the books to the students such that:

- Each student gets at least one book.
- Each student is assigned a **contiguous** block of books.
- Every book is assigned to exactly one student.

Among all valid allocations, minimize the **maximum** number of pages assigned to any single student, and return that minimum value. If allocation is impossible (`k > n`), return `-1`.
questions.title: Allocate Minimum Number of Pages

questions.question:
Given an array of integers `nums` which is sorted in **ascending order**, and an integer `target`, write a function to search `target` in `nums`. If `target` exists, return its **index**. Otherwise, return `-1`.

You must write an algorithm with `O(log n)` runtime complexity.
questions.title: Binary Search
constraints: All integers in nums are unique
nums is sorted in ascending order

questions.question:
The **distance** of a pair of integers `a` and `b` is defined as the absolute difference between `a` and `b`.

Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the **k-th smallest distance among all the pairs** `nums[i]` and `nums[j]` where `0 <= i < j < nums.length`.
questions.title: Find K-th Smallest Pair Distance
constraints: k is 1-indexed (k = 1 is the smallest distance)

questions.question:
Suppose an array of length `n` sorted in ascending order is **rotated** between `1` and `n` times. Given the sorted rotated array `nums` of **unique** elements, return the **minimum element** of this array.

You must write an algorithm that runs in `O(log n)` time.
questions.title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
constraints: All the integers of nums are unique
nums is sorted and rotated between 1 and n times

questions.question:
A peak element is an element that is **strictly greater** than its neighbors.

Given a 0-indexed integer array `nums`, find a peak element, and return its index. If the array contains multiple peaks, return the index to **any** of the peaks.

You may imagine that `nums[-1] = nums[n] = -∞`. In other words, an element is always considered to be strictly greater than a neighbor that is outside the array.

You must write an algorithm that runs in `O(log n)` time.
questions.title: Find Peak Element
constraints: nums[i] != nums[i + 1] for all valid i (no two adjacent values are equal)

questions.question:
Given a sorted (non-decreasing) array `arr` and a value `x`, return the **floor** of `x` (the largest element `≤ x`) and the **ceil** of `x` (the smallest element `≥ x`).

If no floor exists (every element is greater than `x`), return a sentinel such as `−1` for the floor. Likewise return `−1` for the ceil if no element is `≥ x`.
questions.title: Floor and Ceil in a Sorted Array
constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 10⁶, arr sorted in non-decreasing order
Values fit in a 32-bit integer (use long for mid only if indices are huge — here indices fit)
Return a sentinel (−1) when floor or ceil does not exist

questions.question:
Koko loves to eat bananas. There are `n` piles of bananas, the `i`-th pile has `piles[i]` bananas. The guards have gone and will come back in `h` hours.

Koko can decide her bananas-per-hour eating speed of `k`. Each hour, she chooses some pile and eats `k` bananas from it. If the pile has fewer than `k` bananas, she eats all of them and will not eat any more bananas during that hour.

Return the **minimum integer** `k` such that she can eat all the bananas within `h` hours.
questions.title: Koko Eating Bananas

questions.question:
Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the **kth smallest** element in the array.

Note that it is the kth smallest element in sorted order, **not** the kth distinct element — duplicates count toward the rank.
questions.title: Kth Smallest Element in an Array
constraints: Duplicates are allowed and count toward the rank

questions.question:
Given two sorted arrays `nums1` and `nums2` of size `m` and `n` respectively, return **the median** of the two sorted arrays.

The overall run time complexity should be `O(log (m+n))`.
questions.title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays

questions.question:
You are given an array `boards` of `n` integers where `boards[i]` is the length of the i-th board, and an integer `k` — the number of painters.

Each painter paints a **contiguous** sequence of boards, painting 1 unit of board length takes 1 unit of time, and all painters work simultaneously.

Assign the boards so that the time to paint **all** boards is minimized. The total time is the time taken by the painter who finishes last (the largest block of lengths). Return that minimized time.
questions.title: Painter's Partition Problem
constraints: Painters work in parallel; a painter's time equals the sum of lengths in its contiguous block
If a per-unit time t is given, multiply the result by t

questions.question:
Given an array of `n` **distinct** integers and a target value `k`, count the number of unordered pairs of elements whose **difference is exactly k**.

That is, count the pairs `(a, b)` with `a − b = k` (equivalently `|a − b| = k`), where `a` and `b` are two different elements of the array.
questions.title: Pairs

questions.question:
You are given an `m x n` integer matrix `matrix` with the following two properties:

- Each row is sorted in non-decreasing order.
- The first integer of each row is greater than the last integer of the previous row.

Given an integer `target`, return `true` if `target` is in `matrix` or `false` otherwise.

You must write a solution in `O(log(m * n))` time complexity.
questions.title: Search a 2D Matrix

questions.question:
There is an integer array `nums` sorted in ascending order (with **distinct** values). Prior to being passed to your function, `nums` is possibly **rotated** at an unknown pivot index `k` (`0 <= k < nums.length`) so that the resulting array is `[nums[k], nums[k+1], ..., nums[n-1], nums[0], nums[1], ..., nums[k-1]]`.

Given the array `nums` after the possible rotation and an integer `target`, return the **index** of `target` if it is in `nums`, or `-1` if it is not.

You must write an algorithm with `O(log n)` runtime complexity.
questions.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
constraints: All values of nums are unique
nums is an ascending array possibly rotated

questions.question:
Given a sorted array of **distinct** integers `nums` and a target value `target`, return the index if the target is found. If not, return the index where it **would be** if it were inserted in order.

You must write an algorithm with `O(log n)` runtime complexity.
questions.title: Search Insert Position
constraints: nums contains distinct values sorted in ascending order

questions.question:
You are given access to a **unimodal** function `f` over an index range `[0, n−1]` (or a real interval `[lo, hi]`): `f` strictly increases up to a single peak, then strictly decreases. Return the position of the maximum (the peak) and/or its value.

For a unimodal valley (strictly decreasing then increasing), return the minimum instead.
questions.title: Ternary Search on a Unimodal Function
constraints: f is strictly unimodal over the search range (exactly one turning point, no plateaus)
1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁹ for the discrete version; reals use a fixed iteration count
Evaluating f is O(1) (or counted as one query)
For arrays, the peak is strictly greater than its neighbors

questions.question: Given two binary strings `a` and `b`, return *their sum as a binary string*.
questions.title: Add Binary
constraints: a and b consist only of '0' or '1' characters
Each string does not contain leading zeros except for the value '0' itself

questions.question: Given two integers `left` and `right` that represent the range `[left, right]`, return *the bitwise AND of all numbers in this range, inclusive*.
questions.title: Bitwise AND of Numbers Range

questions.question: A binary string `s` of length `n` is encoded as follows: make `k` copies of `s`, shift the j-th copy right by j positions (j = 0..k−1), align them, and XOR each column. The result is an encoded binary string of length `n + k − 1`. Given the encoded string and the integers `n` and `k`, recover and return the original string `s`.
questions.title: Cipher
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁶ (length of the original string s)
Length of the encoded string is exactly n + k − 1
s and the encoded string contain only the characters '0' and '1'

questions.question:
Louise and Richard play a game starting from a counter N. They take turns, Louise first. On each turn the current player does one of two things:

- If N is a power of 2, divide it by 2.
- Otherwise, subtract the largest power of 2 that is less than N.

The player who first makes the counter reach 1 wins. If N is initially 1, Richard wins (Louise never gets to move). Return the name of the winner.
questions.title: Counter Game
constraints: 1 ≤ N < 2⁶⁴ (can exceed 32-bit range — use a 64-bit/unsigned-safe type)
If N == 1 at the start, the winner is Richard

questions.question:
Given an integer `n`, return an array `ans` of length `n + 1` such that for each `i` (`0 ≤ i ≤ n`), `ans[i]` is the **number of 1's** in the binary representation of `i`.

Follow-up: it is very easy to come up with a solution with `O(n log n)` time. Can you do it in **linear time** `O(n)` and possibly in a **single pass**? Can you do it without any built-in function like `__builtin_popcount`?
questions.title: Counting Bits
constraints: Follow-up target: O(n) time, no popcount builtins

questions.question: You are given a list of 32-bit **unsigned** integers. For each integer `n`, flip all 32 of its bits (turn every 1 into a 0 and every 0 into a 1) and return the resulting unsigned decimal value.
questions.title: Flipping Bits
constraints: All 32 bits are flipped, including leading zeros
The result is interpreted as an unsigned 32-bit value

questions.question:
An n-bit **Gray code sequence** is a sequence of `2ⁿ` integers where:

- Every integer is in the inclusive range `[0, 2ⁿ - 1]`,
- The first integer is `0`,
- An integer appears no more than once,
- The binary representations of every pair of **adjacent** integers differ by exactly **one bit**, and
- The binary representations of the **first** and **last** integers also differ by exactly one bit.

Given an integer `n`, return any valid n-bit Gray code sequence.
questions.title: Gray Code Generation
constraints: Multiple valid sequences exist; any correct one is accepted

questions.question:
Given an array of integers where **every element appears exactly twice except for one**, find and return that single element.

Your solution should run in linear time and, ideally, use only constant extra space.
questions.title: Lonely Integer
constraints: Exactly one element appears once; every other appears exactly twice
A unique answer is guaranteed to exist

questions.question: Given two integers `l` and `r`, find the maximum value of `a XOR b` where `a` and `b` satisfy `l ≤ a ≤ b ≤ r`.
questions.title: Maximizing XOR
constraints: a and b are integers with l ≤ a ≤ b ≤ r
a and b may be equal (a == b gives XOR 0)
The answer is a single non-negative integer

questions.question: You are given an array `arr` of non-negative integers and a list of queries. For each query value `x`, find the maximum value of `x XOR arr[i]` over all elements `arr[i]` in the array, and return these maxima in order.
questions.title: Maximum Xor
constraints: Each query is answered independently against the full array

questions.question:
Given an array `nums` containing `n` **distinct** numbers in the range `[0, n]`, return the only number in the range that is **missing** from the array.

Follow-up: could you implement a solution using only `O(1)` extra space complexity and `O(n)` runtime complexity?
questions.title: Missing Number
constraints: All the numbers of nums are unique
Follow-up target: O(n) time, O(1) extra space

questions.question:
Write a function that takes the binary representation of a positive integer and returns the number of `'1'` bits it has (also known as the **Hamming weight**).

Note: in some languages (such as Java) there is no unsigned integer type, so the input is given as a signed integer — its internal binary representation is identical whether it is signed or unsigned.
questions.title: Number of 1 Bits
constraints: In Java the input may be negative (treat the bit pattern as unsigned)
Follow-up: optimise if the function is called many times
Number of set bits ranges from 0 (for 0) to 32 (for all-ones)

questions.question:
Given an integer `n`, return `true` if it is a power of two, otherwise return `false`.

An integer `n` is a power of two if there exists an integer `x` such that `n == 2ˣ`.
questions.title: Power of Two
constraints: n fits in a 32-bit signed integer
x is a non-negative integer (so 1 = 2⁰ counts)

questions.question:
Reverse the bits of a given 32-bit **unsigned** integer.

Note: in some languages (such as Java) there is no unsigned integer type, so the input and output are given as signed integers — they should not affect your implementation, as the internal binary representation is the same whether signed or unsigned.

Follow-up: if this function is called **many times**, how would you optimize it?
questions.title: Reverse Bits
constraints: The input is a 32-bit unsigned integer
In Java the value is given as a signed int (same bit pattern)
Follow-up: optimize for many repeated calls (caching)

questions.question: Given an array `arr` of `n` integers, consider the XOR of the elements of every contiguous subarray. XOR all of those subarray-XOR values together and return the single resulting value.
questions.title: Sansa and XOR
constraints: 0 ≤ arr[i] ≤ 10⁸ (roughly; fits comfortably in a 32-bit int)

questions.question:
Given a **non-empty** array of integers `nums`, every element appears **twice** except for one. Find that single one.

You must implement a solution with **linear runtime complexity** and use only **constant extra space**.
questions.title: Single Number
constraints: Each element appears exactly twice except one element which appears once
Required: O(n) time and O(1) extra space

questions.question:
You are given an integer `n` and an array `A` of length `2ⁿ`, where `A[s]` is a value associated with the bitmask `s` (a subset of an n-element ground set).

For every mask `m` in `[0, 2ⁿ - 1]`, compute `F[m] = Σ A[s]` over **all submasks** `s` of `m` (every `s` with `s & m == s`).

Return the array `F`.
questions.title: Sum Over Subsets (SOS DP)
constraints: Values fit in a 64-bit integer (use long / Python int)
A submask s of m satisfies (s & m) == s; m is a submask of itself, and 0 is a submask of every m

questions.question:
The **XOR total** of an array is the bitwise XOR of all its elements; the XOR total of an empty array is `0`.

Given an array `nums`, return the sum of the XOR totals of **every subset** of `nums`. Subsets with the same elements but different indices are counted separately.
questions.title: Sum of All Subset XOR Totals
constraints: There are 2ⁿ subsets, including the empty subset

questions.question: Given two integers `a` and `b`, return the sum of the two integers **without using the operators `+` and `-`**.
questions.title: Sum of Two Integers
constraints: Result fits in a signed 32-bit integer
Bitwise operators (^, &, |, ~, <<, >>) and loops are allowed

questions.question:
Given an integer `n`, count the number of integers `x` satisfying `0 ≤ x ≤ n` such that `n + x == n ^ x`, where `^` is the bitwise XOR.

Return that count.
questions.title: Sum vs XOR
constraints: x ranges over the inclusive interval [0, n]
n + x uses ordinary integer addition; n ^ x is bitwise XOR
The answer can be large, so use a 64-bit type

questions.question:
You are given two strings, `a` and `b`. You can perform the following operations on string `a`:

1. **Capitalize** zero or more of `a`'s lowercase letters.
2. **Delete** all of the remaining lowercase letters in `a`.

Given `a` and `b`, determine whether it is possible to make `a` **equal to** `b` using these operations. Note that `b` consists only of uppercase letters, and the uppercase letters already present in `a` can be neither deleted nor altered.

Return `"YES"` if `a` can be transformed into `b`, otherwise `"NO"`.
questions.title: Abbreviation
constraints: `a` consists of uppercase and lowercase English letters
`b` consists only of uppercase English letters
Uppercase letters in `a` cannot be deleted or changed
Lowercase letters in `a` may each be capitalized or deleted

questions.question:
You are given a boolean expression as a string with operands `T` (true) and `F` (false) separated by the binary operators `&` (AND), `|` (OR), and `^` (XOR). For example: `T|T&F^T`.

Count the number of ways to fully **parenthesize** the expression so that it evaluates to ***true***. Two parenthesizations are different if their bracketing differs.

Return that count. (By the classic convention the answer is taken modulo `1003`.)
questions.title: Boolean Parenthesization
constraints: 1 ≤ number of operands ≤ ~100 (string length is odd: operands at even indices, operators at odd)
Operands are exactly T or F
Counts can grow large → take the result modulo 1003 (the standard variant)

questions.question:
Alice is a teacher with `n` students standing in a line, each with a rating. She wants to give candies subject to two rules:

1. Every student must receive **at least one** candy.
2. Any student with a **strictly higher** rating than an immediate neighbour must receive **strictly more** candies than that neighbour.

Given the array of ratings, return the **minimum** total number of candies Alice must distribute.
questions.title: Candies
constraints: Only strictly-greater ratings impose a constraint; equal-rated neighbours are unconstrained relative to each other
Every child receives at least one candy

questions.question:
You are climbing a staircase. It takes `n` steps to reach the top.

Each time you can either climb **1** or **2** steps. In how many ***distinct ways*** can you climb to the top?

Return the total number of distinct ways as an integer.
questions.title: Climbing Stairs
constraints: The answer fits in a 32-bit signed integer for all valid n

questions.question:
You are given an integer array `coins` representing coins of different denominations and an integer `amount` representing a total amount of money.

Return the ***fewest number of coins*** that you need to make up that amount. If that amount of money **cannot** be made up by any combination of the coins, return `-1`.

You may assume that you have an ***infinite*** number of each kind of coin.
questions.title: Coin Change

questions.question:
A string is said to be a **child** of another string if it can be formed by **deleting zero or more characters** from the parent (the remaining characters keep their original order). In other words, a child is a subsequence.

Given two strings `s1` and `s2` of equal length consisting of uppercase English letters, find the **length of the longest string** that is a child of *both* `s1` and `s2`.
questions.title: Common Child
constraints: Both strings contain only uppercase English letters A–Z
Return the length of the longest common child (a subsequence, not a substring)

questions.question:
Consider an array of `n` integers, where each element is between `1` and `k` (inclusive). You must build such an array subject to:

1. The **first** element is `1` (a[0] = 1).
2. The **last** element is `x` (a[n−1] = x).
3. Every pair of **consecutive** elements is **different** (a[i] ≠ a[i−1]).

Return the number of such arrays, **modulo 1e9 + 7**.
questions.title: Construct the Array

questions.question:
You are given an `m × n` integer grid where `grid[i][j] = 0` means the cell is free and `grid[i][j] = 1` means it is blocked by an obstacle.

A robot starts at the **top-left** cell `(0, 0)` and wants to reach the **bottom-right** cell `(m-1, n-1)`. It can move only **right** or **down** at each step, and it cannot enter a blocked cell.

Return the ***number of distinct paths*** the robot can take. If the start or destination is blocked, the answer is `0`.
questions.title: Count Paths in a Grid with Obstacles
constraints: Moves are restricted to right and down
The path count can be large but fits in a 64-bit integer for these bounds

questions.question:
A **decibinary** number is written with decimal digits (0–9) but each position carries a power-of-two weight, so a decibinary numeral `d_k … d_1 d_0` has decimal value `Σ d_i · 2^i`. Because digits go up to 9, many distinct decibinary numerals share the same decimal value (e.g. decimal 4 is `4`, `12`, `20`, `100`).

Consider **all** decibinary numbers listed in increasing order, sorted first by their **decimal value** and, within the same value, by the **decibinary numeral** itself (numerically). The list begins: `0` (=0), `1` (=1), `2` and `10` (=2), `3` and `11` (=3), `4`, `12`, `20`, `100` (=4), …

Given `q` queries, each an index `x` (1-based), return the decibinary numeral at position `x` in this list.
questions.title: Decibinary Numbers
constraints: 1 ≤ x ≤ 10^16 (1-based index into the global ordered list)
Indexing starts at 1; position 1 is the numeral 0 (decimal value 0)
Counts of numerals per value can reach ~10^16 — use 64-bit integers
Return the decibinary numeral as a string/number, without leading zeros

questions.question:
A message containing letters from `A-Z` is encoded to numbers using the mapping `'A' -> "1"`, `'B' -> "2"`, …, `'Z' -> "26"`.

To **decode** an encoded message, all the digits must be grouped then mapped back into letters using the **reverse** of this mapping (there may be multiple valid groupings).

Given a string `s` containing only digits, return **the number of ways to decode it**. Note that `'06'` cannot map to `'F'` because `'6'` is different from `'06'`. The answer fits in a 32-bit integer.
questions.title: Decode Ways
constraints: s contains only digits and may contain leading zeros
A grouping starting with '0' is invalid (no letter maps to 0 or to '0x')
Valid two-digit groups are exactly '10' through '26'

questions.question:
Given two strings `word1` and `word2`, return the ***minimum number of operations*** required to convert `word1` to `word2`.

You have the following three operations permitted on a word:

- **Insert** a character
- **Delete** a character
- **Replace** a character
questions.title: Edit Distance
constraints: word1 and word2 consist of lowercase English letters

questions.question:
You are given `k` identical eggs and a building with `n` floors numbered `1` to `n`.

There exists a ***critical floor*** `f` (with `0 ≤ f ≤ n`) such that any egg dropped from a floor **above** `f` breaks, and any egg dropped from floor `f` or **below** survives. An unbroken egg can be reused; a broken egg cannot.

You want to determine `f` with certainty. Each move, you drop an egg from a floor of your choice and observe whether it breaks. Return the ***minimum number of drops*** that guarantees you can identify `f` in the ***worst case***, no matter where `f` actually is.
questions.title: Egg Dropping Puzzle
constraints: The critical floor f is fixed but unknown; you must guarantee detection

questions.question:
Karen wants to make all of her colleagues' chocolate counts **equal**. In a single operation she may add `1`, `2`, or `5` chocolates to **all colleagues except one** of her choosing.

Given the initial array of chocolate counts, return the **minimum number of operations** needed to make every colleague's count equal.
questions.title: Equal
constraints: Each operation adds exactly 1, 2, or 5 to all-but-one element
Multiple test cases may be batched

questions.question:
A series is defined as follows:

`t(i+2) = t(i) + (t(i+1))²`

with given first two terms `t₁` and `t₂`. Given three integers `t₁`, `t₂`, and `n`, compute and return the value of the **nth term**, `tₙ`.

Because the terms grow extremely quickly, the result may be a very large number and must be computed exactly.
questions.title: Fibonacci Modified
constraints: Terms grow doubly-exponentially — the answer can have thousands of digits
The result must be exact (use arbitrary-precision integers)

questions.question:
A modified Fibonacci sequence is defined by:

    t(i+2) = t(i) + (t(i+1))²

Given three integers `t1`, `t2`, and `n`, compute and return the `n`-th term of the sequence (1-indexed), where `t1` and `t2` are the first two terms.
questions.title: Fibonacci Modified
constraints: The terms grow doubly-exponentially — the n-th term can have thousands of digits
Return the exact value (arbitrary precision); no modulus is applied

questions.question:
Gena has a Towers of Hanoi setup with **4 pegs** and `n` disks of distinct sizes (disk 1 is the smallest, disk `n` the largest). You're given the starting peg of each disk in an arbitrary (but legal) configuration.

As in standard Hanoi, you may move the **topmost** disk of any peg onto another peg, but only if the destination peg is empty or its top disk is **larger** than the one being moved. Find the **minimum number of moves** required to stack all `n` disks onto **peg 1**.
questions.title: Gena Playing Hanoi
constraints: Disk i has size i; only the smallest disk on a peg (its top) can be moved
A disk may be placed only on an empty peg or on a strictly larger disk
The starting configuration is legal; goal is all disks on peg 1

questions.question:
You are a professional robber planning to rob houses along a street. This time the houses are arranged in a **circle** — the first and last houses are ***adjacent*** to each other.

As before, adjacent houses have connected security systems, so robbing two directly adjacent houses on the same night alerts the police.

Given the integer array `nums` of money in each house, return the ***maximum amount you can rob tonight without alerting the police***.
questions.title: House Robber II

questions.question:
You are a professional robber planning to rob houses along a street. Each house has a certain amount of money stashed, given by the array `nums`.

The only constraint stopping you is that **adjacent houses have connected security systems** — robbing two directly adjacent houses on the same night will automatically alert the police.

Return the ***maximum amount of money*** you can rob tonight without alerting the police.
questions.title: House Robber

questions.question:
Given two strings `text1` and `text2`, return the length of their **longest common subsequence**. If there is no common subsequence, return `0`.

A **subsequence** of a string is a new string generated from the original string with some characters (can be none) deleted ***without changing the relative order*** of the remaining characters.

A **common subsequence** of two strings is a subsequence that is common to both strings.
questions.title: Longest Common Subsequence
constraints: text1 and text2 consist of lowercase English characters only
Order of characters must be preserved (subsequence, not subset)

questions.question:
Given an integer array `nums`, return **the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence**.

A **subsequence** is a sequence derivable from the array by deleting some or no elements **without changing the order** of the remaining elements. For example, `[3, 6, 2, 7]` is a subsequence of `[0, 3, 1, 6, 2, 2, 7]`.

The subsequence must be **strictly** increasing — equal adjacent values do not count.
questions.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
constraints: The subsequence need NOT be contiguous (it's a subsequence, not a subarray)
Increasing means strictly increasing — duplicates cannot both be included

questions.question:
Given a string `s`, find the length of the ***longest palindromic subsequence*** in `s`.

A **subsequence** is a sequence derived from `s` by deleting zero or more characters without changing the order of the remaining characters. A **palindrome** reads the same forwards and backwards.

Return the length of the longest such subsequence (you do not need to return the subsequence itself).
questions.title: Longest Palindromic Subsequence
constraints: s consists only of lowercase English letters
The answer is at least 1 (any single character is a palindrome of length 1)

questions.question:
Given a string `s`, return **the longest palindromic substring** in `s`.

A **palindrome** is a string that reads the same forwards and backwards. A **substring** is a contiguous sequence of characters within the string.

If there are multiple answers of the same maximum length, returning any one of them is accepted.
questions.title: Longest Palindromic Substring
constraints: s consists of only digits and English letters
The answer is always a contiguous substring, never a subsequence
At least one palindrome always exists (any single character)

questions.question:
You are given an array `p` of length `n + 1` describing the dimensions of `n` matrices: matrix `i` (for `i` from `1` to `n`) has dimensions `p[i-1] × p[i]`, so adjacent matrices are conformable for multiplication.

Matrix multiplication is associative, so the *result* is the same for any parenthesization, but the ***number of scalar multiplications*** differs. Multiplying an `a × b` matrix by a `b × c` matrix costs `a · b · c` scalar multiplications.

Return the ***minimum*** number of scalar multiplications needed to compute the product of the whole chain.
questions.title: Matrix Chain Multiplication

questions.question:
Given an array of integers, find the **maximum sum of a subset** such that **no two chosen elements are adjacent** in the array.

You may skip as many elements as you like; the only restriction is that you cannot pick two elements that sit next to each other. Elements may be negative, so the optimal subset is not simply 'all the positives'.

Return the maximum achievable sum.
questions.title: Max Array Sum
constraints: The chosen subset may be empty in some variants; here the recurrence allows a single element to stand alone

questions.question:
Given an `m x n` binary `matrix` filled with `0`s and `1`s, find the largest **square** containing only `1`s and return ***its area***.

The matrix entries are given as the characters `'0'` and `'1'`.
questions.title: Maximal Square

questions.question:
Given an integer array `nums`, find a **contiguous non-empty subarray** within the array that has the **largest product**, and return *the product*.

The test cases are generated so that the answer fits in a **32-bit integer**.

A **subarray** is a contiguous, non-empty sequence of elements within an array.
questions.title: Maximum Product Subarray
constraints: The product of any prefix is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit integer
The subarray must be contiguous and non-empty

questions.question:
Given a ***circular integer array*** `nums` of length `n`, return the **maximum possible sum of a non-empty subarray** of `nums`.

A *circular array* means the end of the array connects to the beginning: formally, the next element of `nums[i]` is `nums[(i + 1) % n]`.

A *subarray* may only include each element of the fixed buffer `nums` **at most once**: formally, for a subarray `nums[i], nums[i+1], ..., nums[j]`, there does not exist `i <= k1, k2 <= j` with `k1 % n == k2 % n`.
questions.title: Maximum Sum Circular Subarray
constraints: The subarray must be non-empty and use each buffer index at most once

questions.question:
Given a `m x n` `grid` filled with non-negative numbers, find a path from the **top-left** to the **bottom-right** which ***minimizes the sum*** of all numbers along its path.

You can only move either **down** or **right** at any point in time.
questions.title: Minimum Path Sum

questions.question:
Given a string `s`, return **the number of palindromic substrings** in it.

A **substring** is a contiguous sequence of characters within the string. Two substrings are counted separately if they start or end at different indices, **even if they consist of the same characters**.

Every single character is a palindrome, so the answer is at least `s.length`.
questions.title: Palindromic Substrings
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
Substrings at different index ranges count separately even if equal as strings
The answer fits comfortably in a 32-bit integer (max ~500500 for n = 1000)

questions.question:
There are `n` users registered on a website, each with a known password. The passwords are given as a list of lowercase strings. An attacker has concatenated some of these passwords (each may be used any number of times, in any order) into a single login attempt string with no separators.

Given the list of passwords and the login attempt, determine whether the attempt can be formed by concatenating passwords. If it can, return the sequence of passwords (in order, space-separated) that forms it; otherwise return the string `WRONG PASSWORD`.
questions.title: Password Cracker

examples.input: passwords = [because, can, do, must, we, what], attempt = "wedowhatwemustbecausewecan"
examples.output: we do what we must because we can

constraints: 1 ≤ length of the login attempt ≤ 2000 (concatenation of one or more passwords)
All strings are lowercase English letters; passwords are reusable

questions.question:
Davis has a number of staircases, and he can climb exactly **1, 2, or 3** steps at a time. Given the number of steps `n` in a staircase, count the total number of distinct ways Davis can climb to the top.

Because the count grows quickly, return the answer **modulo 10000000007** (that is, 10¹⁰ + 7).
questions.title: Davis' Staircase
constraints: Davis may ascend by exactly 1, 2, or 3 steps in a single move

questions.question:
Red John has created a program that tiles a wall of size **4 × n** using bricks of size **4 × 1** (which may be placed vertically or horizontally). Let `M` be the number of distinct ways to completely tile the wall.

Your task: compute `M`, then determine **how many prime numbers are less than or equal to `M`**. Return that prime count.
questions.title: Red John is Back
constraints: Bricks are 4×1 and tile a 4×n wall completely without overlap
M is the number of distinct tilings
The answer is the count of primes p with p ≤ M

questions.question:
You are given a rod of length `n` and an array `price` where `price[i]` is the price of a piece of length `i` (for `i` from `1` to `n`).

Cut the rod into one or more pieces (or leave it whole) to ***maximize the total price*** you can earn. You may cut as many pieces of any length as you like; equal-length pieces always earn the same price.

Return the maximum obtainable price.
questions.title: Rod Cutting
constraints: price has a defined value for every length 1..n

questions.question:
Given an integer represented as a **string** of digits, consider every **substring** of it as a number. Compute the **sum of all these substring values**, and return it **modulo 1e9 + 7**.

For example, for the string `"16"` the substrings are `"1"`, `"6"`, and `"16"`, i.e. the numbers 1, 6, and 16, summing to 23.
questions.title: Sam and Substrings
constraints: s consists of decimal digits (it may contain leading zeros in substrings)
The answer can be enormous → return it modulo 1 000 000 007

questions.question:
You are given an array `A` of `n` integers. Construct an array `B` of the same length where each element satisfies `1 ≤ B[i] ≤ A[i]`.

Define the **cost** as:

`S = Σ |B[i] − B[i−1]|` for `i` from 1 to n−1.

Return the **maximum** possible value of `S` over all valid arrays `B`.
questions.title: Sherlock and Cost
constraints: Each B[i] is an integer with 1 ≤ B[i] ≤ A[i]
Cost is the sum of absolute differences of consecutive B values

questions.question:
You are given an array `nums` of positive integers and a target integer `T`.

Determine whether there exists a ***subset*** of `nums` whose elements sum to exactly `T`. Each element may be used **at most once** (it's either in the subset or not).

Return `true` if such a subset exists, otherwise `false`.
questions.title: Subset Sum

questions.question:
You are given an integer `amount` and an array `coins` of distinct denominations, each available in **unlimited** quantity.

Count the number of **distinct combinations** of coins whose values sum exactly to `amount`. Two combinations are the same if they use the same multiset of coins — order does **not** matter, so `1 + 2` and `2 + 1` count as a single way.

Return the number of such combinations. If no combination sums to `amount`, return 0.
questions.title: The Coin Change Problem
constraints: Each coin may be used an unlimited number of times
The answer fits in a 64-bit / Python int

questions.question:
Given a `triangle` array, return the ***minimum path sum*** from top to bottom.

For each step, you may move to an **adjacent** number of the row below. More formally, if you are on index `i` of the current row, you may move to either index `i` or index `i + 1` of the next row.
questions.title: Triangle
constraints: Follow-up: can you use only O(n) extra space, where n is the number of rows?

questions.question:
You are given `n` item types, where type `i` has a positive `weight[i]` and a positive `value[i]`, and a knapsack of maximum weight capacity `W`.

Maximize the total value of items placed in the knapsack without exceeding `W`. Unlike 0/1 knapsack, you may use each item type an ***unlimited number of times*** (any non-negative count of each).

Return the maximum total value achievable.
questions.title: Unbounded Knapsack
constraints: All weights and values are integers

questions.question:
A robot is located at the **top-left** corner of an `m x n` grid. The robot can only move either **down** or **right** at any point in time.

The robot is trying to reach the **bottom-right** corner of the grid.

How many ***possible unique paths*** are there?
questions.title: Unique Paths
constraints: The answer is guaranteed to be ≤ 2 × 10⁹ (fits in a 32-bit-ish range / Java int is safe)
The robot moves only right or down — never up or left
Start is grid[0][0], destination is grid[m-1][n-1]

questions.question:
Given an input string `s` and a pattern `p`, implement wildcard matching that supports:

- `'?'` — matches any **single** character.
- `'*'` — matches any sequence of characters, **including the empty sequence**.

The match must cover the ***entire*** input string `s` (not a partial match). Return `true` if `p` matches `s`, otherwise `false`.

Here `s` contains only lowercase letters; `p` contains lowercase letters, `'?'`, and `'*'`.
questions.title: Wildcard Matching
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
'*' matches any sequence including empty; '?' matches exactly one character

questions.question:
Given a string `s` and a dictionary of strings `wordDict`, return `true` if `s` can be **segmented** into a space-separated sequence of one or more dictionary words.

**Note:** the same dictionary word may be reused ***multiple times*** in the segmentation.
questions.title: Word Break
constraints: s and wordDict[i] consist of only lowercase English letters
All the strings of wordDict are unique

questions.question:
You are given `n` items, where item `i` has a positive weight `weight[i]` and a positive value `value[i]`, and a knapsack with a maximum weight capacity `W`.

Choose a ***subset*** of the items so that the total weight is at most `W` and the ***total value is maximized***. Each item may be used **at most once** (you either take it whole or leave it — no fractions, no repeats).

Return the maximum total value achievable.
questions.title: 0/1 Knapsack
constraints: All weights and values are integers

questions.question:
You are given a weighted directed graph with `n` vertices labeled `0` to `n - 1`, an edge list where `edges[i] = [u, v, w]` (weight `w` may be negative), and a source `src`.

Return an array `dist` where `dist[i]` is the shortest-path distance from `src` to `i`, or `-1` if `i` is unreachable. If the graph contains a negative-weight cycle reachable from `src`, return an empty array `[]` to signal that shortest paths are undefined.
questions.title: Bellman-Ford Shortest Path

questions.question:
You are given an undirected graph of `n` nodes (labeled `1` to `n`) and a list of edges. Every edge has the **same weight, 6**. From a given start node `s`, return an array of the shortest distances to each of the other `n − 1` nodes (in increasing node order, skipping `s`).

If a node is unreachable from `s`, its distance is `-1`.
questions.title: BFS: Shortest Reach in a Graph
constraints: The graph is undirected and may be disconnected

questions.question:
There is an undirected graph with `n` nodes, where each node is labeled `0` to `n - 1`. You are given a 2D array `graph`, where `graph[u]` is the list of nodes adjacent to node `u`.
