The graph is **bipartite** if you can split its nodes into two independent sets `A` and `B` so that every edge connects a node in `A` to a node in `B`.

Return `true` if and only if the graph is bipartite.
questions.title: Is Graph Bipartite? (Two-Coloring)
constraints: graph[u] does not contain u (no self-loops)
The graph may not be connected
If v is in graph[u], then u is in graph[v] (undirected)

questions.question:
You are given an `N × N` grid where each cell is `.` (open) or `X` (blocked), plus a start position `(startRow, startCol)` and a goal `(goalRow, goalCol)`. A **move** picks one of the four directions (up, down, left, right) and slides the piece across consecutive open cells until it is stopped by the grid border or a blocked cell — you may stop at any open cell along that line, and the entire slide counts as **one move**.

Return the **minimum number of moves** to get from the start to the goal.
questions.title: Castle on the Grid
constraints: Start and goal are open cells; they may coincide (answer 0)
Coordinates are 0-indexed: (row, col), row downward, col rightward
A path from start to goal always exists for the given inputs

questions.title: Clone Graph
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 100]
There are no repeated edges and no self-loops
The graph is connected and all nodes can be reached from the given node

questions.question:
There are `2 × N` nodes in an undirected graph, labeled `1` to `2N`. Each edge connects a node from the left set (`1..N`) to a node from the right set (`N+1..2N`). You are given a list of `edges`.

Return two values: the size of the **smallest** connected component and the size of the **largest** connected component, considering only components that contain at least two nodes.
questions.title: Components in a Graph
constraints: Each edge's left endpoint is in 1..N, right endpoint in N+1..2N
The graph is undirected; isolated nodes (in no edge) are ignored
At least one edge exists, so at least one component of size ≥ 2 exists

questions.question:
There are a total of `numCourses` courses you have to take, labeled from `0` to `numCourses - 1`. You are given an array `prerequisites` where `prerequisites[i] = [aᵢ, bᵢ]` indicates that you **must take course `bᵢ` first** if you want to take course `aᵢ`.

Return *the ordering of courses you should take to finish all courses*. If there are many valid answers, return **any** of them. If it is impossible to finish all courses, return **an empty array**.
questions.title: Course Schedule II
constraints: All the pairs [aᵢ, bᵢ] are distinct

questions.question:
There are a total of `numCourses` courses you have to take, labeled from `0` to `numCourses - 1`. You are given an array `prerequisites` where `prerequisites[i] = [aᵢ, bᵢ]` indicates that you **must take course `bᵢ` first** if you want to take course `aᵢ`.

Return `true` if you can finish all courses. Otherwise, return `false`.
questions.title: Course Schedule (Topological Sort)
constraints: All the pairs prerequisites[i] are distinct

questions.question:
You are given a directed graph with `n` nodes labeled `0` to `n - 1`, described by an edge list `edges` where `edges[i] = [u, v]` is a directed edge `u → v`.

Return `true` if the graph contains at least one cycle, and `false` otherwise.
questions.title: Detect Cycle in a Directed Graph
constraints: The graph may be disconnected and may contain self-loops

questions.question:
You are given a weighted directed graph with `n` vertices labeled `0` to `n - 1`, a list of edges where `edges[i] = [u, v, w]` means an edge from `u` to `v` with weight `w ≥ 0`, and a source vertex `src`.

Return an array `dist` where `dist[i]` is the **length of the shortest path** from `src` to vertex `i`, or `Infinity` (represented as `-1` in the output) if `i` is unreachable.
questions.title: Dijkstra's Shortest Path

questions.question:
You are given an undirected graph of `n` nodes (labeled `1` to `n`) and a list of weighted edges where `edges[i] = [u, v, w]` is an edge between `u` and `v` of weight `w ≥ 0`. There may be multiple edges between the same pair of nodes.

Given a start node `s`, return the shortest distance from `s` to every **other** node (in increasing node order, skipping `s`). If a node is unreachable, its distance is `-1`.
questions.title: Dijkstra: Shortest Reach 2
constraints: The graph is undirected and may be disconnected

questions.question:
You are given a tree (a connected, acyclic, undirected graph) of `N` nodes labeled `1` to `N`, rooted at node `1`, described by a list of `edges`. `N` is even.

Remove as many edges as possible so that every resulting connected component has an **even** number of nodes. Return the **maximum number of edges** you can remove.
questions.title: Even Tree
constraints: The graph is a tree: exactly N − 1 edges, connected, acyclic
Nodes are labeled 1 to N, rooted at node 1
Edges are undirected; build the tree by skipping the parent when recursing
A valid partition always exists because N is even

questions.question:
You are given an undirected, unweighted graph of `n` nodes (labeled `1` to `n`) described by two parallel edge lists `graphFrom` and `graphTo`. Each node `i` carries a color `ids[i]`.

Given a target color `val`, return the **minimum number of edges** on a path connecting two distinct nodes that both have color `val`. If fewer than two nodes have color `val`, or no two such nodes are connected, return `-1`.
questions.title: Find the Nearest Clone
constraints: The graph is undirected and may be disconnected
There may be 0, 1, or many nodes with the target color

questions.question:
You are given a directed weighted graph of `n` nodes (labeled `1` to `n`) with edges `edges[i] = [u, v, w]` meaning a directed road from `u` to `v` of length `w`. Then you are given `q` queries; each query `(a, b)` asks for the **length of the shortest path** from `a` to `b`.

For each query, return the shortest distance, or `-1` if `b` is unreachable from `a`.
questions.title: Floyd: City of Blinding Lights
constraints: The graph is directed; parallel edges may appear (keep the minimum)

questions.question:
You are given an integer `n` and a list of weighted directed edges `edges[i] = [u, v, w]` for a graph on vertices `0..n-1`. Weights may be negative but assume no negative cycle.

Return an `n × n` matrix `dist` where `dist[i][j]` is the shortest-path distance from `i` to `j`, `0` when `i == j`, and `-1` when `j` is unreachable from `i`.
questions.title: Floyd-Warshall All-Pairs Shortest Path
constraints: -10⁴ ≤ w ≤ 10⁴ (weights may be negative; no negative cycle)
There may be at most one directed edge per ordered pair

questions.question:
You are given a list of `q` queries. Each query is a pair `(a, b)` declaring that persons `a` and `b` are now friends. Friendship is **transitive**: if `a`–`b` and `b`–`c` are friends, then `a`, `b`, `c` form one friend circle.

After processing each query, record the size of the **largest friend circle** that exists at that moment. Return the list of these maxima, one per query.
questions.title: Friend Circle Queries
constraints: 1 ≤ a, b ≤ 10⁹ (person IDs are large and sparse)
a ≠ b within a query (or, if equal, the union is a harmless no-op)
Friendships are permanent and undirected (never removed)
Output has exactly q entries — the running max after each query

questions.question:
You have a graph of `n` nodes labeled from `0` to `n - 1`. You are given an integer `n` and a list of `edges` where `edges[i] = [aᵢ, bᵢ]` indicates that there is an **undirected** edge between nodes `aᵢ` and `bᵢ` in the graph.

Return `true` if the edges of the given graph make up a **valid tree**, and `false` otherwise.
questions.title: Graph Valid Tree

questions.question:
There are `N` astronauts numbered `0` to `N − 1`. A list of `pairs` tells you which astronauts are from the **same** country: `pairs[i] = [a, b]` means astronaut `a` and astronaut `b` share a country (this relation is transitive — if `a` and `b` are countrymen and `b` and `c` are, then so are `a` and `c`).

The space agency wants to send **two astronauts from different countries** to the moon. Return the number of ways to choose such a pair.
questions.title: Journey to the Moon
constraints: The same-country relation is transitive (it forms connected components)
The answer can exceed 32-bit range — use 64-bit

questions.question:
You are given `n` vertices labeled `0` to `n - 1` and a list of undirected weighted edges `edges[i] = [u, v, w]`.

Return the **total weight of a minimum spanning tree** — the cheapest set of edges that connects all `n` vertices with no cycle. If the graph is not connected (no spanning tree exists), return `-1`.
questions.title: Kruskal's Minimum Spanning Tree
constraints: The graph is undirected and may contain parallel edges

questions.question:
Given an undirected weighted graph with `n` nodes (labeled `1` to `n`) and a list of edges where `edges[i] = [u, v, w]` connects `u` and `v` with weight `w`, find the total weight of its **Minimum Spanning Tree** — the subset of edges that connects all `n` nodes with the smallest possible total weight and no cycles.

The graph is connected. If multiple edges connect the same pair, the smallest qualifying one is naturally chosen. Return a single integer: the MST's total weight.
questions.title: Kruskal (MST): Really Special Subtree
constraints: The graph is connected and undirected; parallel edges and self-loops may appear
A spanning tree always exists (the graph is connected)

questions.question:
A gene string can be represented by an 8-character long string, with choices from `'A'`, `'C'`, `'G'`, and `'T'`.

Suppose we need to investigate a mutation from a gene string `startGene` to a gene string `endGene` where one mutation is defined as **one single character** changed in the gene string.

- For example, `"AACCGGTT" --> "AACCGGTA"` is one mutation.

There is also a gene `bank` that records all the valid gene mutations. A gene must be in `bank` to make it a valid gene string.

Given the two gene strings `startGene` and `endGene` and the gene `bank`, return *the minimum number of mutations needed to mutate from `startGene` to `endGene`*. If there is no such a mutation, return `-1`.

Note that the starting point is assumed to be valid, so it might not be included in the bank.
questions.title: Minimum Genetic Mutation
constraints: startGene, endGene, and bank[i] consist of only the characters ['A', 'C', 'G', 'T']

questions.question:
You have a graph of `n` nodes labelled from `0` to `n - 1`. You are given an integer `n` and an array `edges` where `edges[i] = [aᵢ, bᵢ]` indicates that there is an **undirected** edge between nodes `aᵢ` and `bᵢ` in the graph.

Return ***the number of connected components*** in the graph.
questions.title: Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph

questions.question:
Given an `m x n` 2D binary grid `grid` which represents a map of `'1'`s (land) and `'0'`s (water), return **the number of islands**.

An **island** is surrounded by water and is formed by connecting adjacent lands horizontally or vertically. You may assume all four edges of the grid are surrounded by water.
questions.title: Number of Islands

questions.question:
There is an `m x n` rectangular island that borders both the **Pacific Ocean** and **Atlantic Ocean**. The Pacific Ocean touches the island's left and top edges, and the Atlantic Ocean touches the island's right and bottom edges.

The island is partitioned into a grid of square cells. You are given an `m x n` integer matrix `heights` where `heights[r][c]` represents the height above sea level of the cell at `(r, c)`.

The island receives a lot of rain, and rain water can flow to neighboring cells directly north, south, east, and west if the neighboring cell's height is **less than or equal to** the current cell's height. Water can flow from any cell adjacent to an ocean into the ocean.

Return a list of grid coordinates where water can flow to **both** the Pacific and Atlantic oceans.
questions.title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow

questions.question:
You are given `n` vertices labeled `0` to `n - 1` and a list of undirected weighted edges `edges[i] = [u, v, w]`.

Return the **total weight of a minimum spanning tree** — the cheapest set of edges connecting all `n` vertices with no cycle. If the graph is not connected, return `-1`.
questions.title: Prim's Minimum Spanning Tree
constraints: The graph is undirected and may contain parallel edges

questions.question:
Given an undirected weighted graph with `n` nodes (labeled `1` to `n`), a list of edges `edges[i] = [u, v, w]`, and a **start node** `start`, find the total weight of the **Minimum Spanning Tree** built by Prim's algorithm.

The graph is connected, so a spanning tree exists. If multiple edges join the same pair, the cheapest is effectively used. Return a single integer: the total weight of the MST.
questions.title: Prim's (MST): Special Subtree
constraints: The graph is connected and undirected; parallel edges and self-loops may appear

questions.question:
The HackerLand government wants every citizen to have access to a library. There are `n` cities (numbered `1` to `n`) and a list of bidirectional `roads` that could be repaired, where `roads[i] = [u, v]` means a road can be repaired between city `u` and city `v`.

Building a library in a city costs `c_lib`. Repairing one road costs `c_road`. A city has access to a library if it contains one, or if it is connected through repaired roads to a city that contains one.

Return the **minimum total cost** to give every city access to a library.
questions.title: Roads and Libraries
constraints: Roads are bidirectional; the graph may be disconnected
The answer can exceed 32-bit range — use 64-bit

questions.question:
You are given an `m x n` grid where each cell can have one of three values:
- `0` representing an empty cell,
- `1` representing a fresh orange, or
- `2` representing a rotten orange.

Every minute, any fresh orange that is **4-directionally adjacent** to a rotten orange becomes rotten.

Return the **minimum number of minutes** that must elapse until no cell has a fresh orange. If this is impossible, return `-1`.
questions.title: Rotting Oranges

questions.question:
You play on a board of squares numbered `1` to `100`. You start on square `1`. On each turn you roll a die and advance `1` to `6` squares. Some squares are connected by **ladders** (climb up: landing on the foot moves you to the top) and **snakes** (slide down: landing on the mouth moves you to the tail).

Given the ladders and snakes, return the **minimum number of dice rolls** to reach square `100` from square `1`, or `-1` if it cannot be reached.
questions.title: Snakes and Ladders: The Quickest Way Up
constraints: The board always has exactly 100 squares
0 ≤ ladders.length, snakes.length (each is a [start, end] pair)
Ladder start < ladder end; snake start > snake end
No square is the start of more than one snake or ladder
Squares 1 and 100 are never a snake or ladder endpoint that conflicts with the rules

questions.question:
You are given an `n x n` integer matrix `board` where the cells are labeled from `1` to `n²` in a **Boustrophedon style** starting from the bottom left of the board (i.e. `board[n - 1][0]`) and alternating direction each row.

You start on square `1`. In each move, starting from square `curr`, you may choose a destination square `next` with a label in the range `[curr + 1, min(curr + 6, n²)]` (simulating a 6-sided die). If `board[r][c] != -1`, the square has a snake or ladder and you must move to `board[r][c]` (you do not roll again).

Return *the least number of moves required to reach the square `n²`*. If it is not possible to reach the square, return `-1`.
questions.title: Snakes and Ladders
constraints: grid[i][j] is either -1 or in the range [1, n²]
The squares labeled 1 and n² do not have any ladders or snakes

questions.question:
Given an `m x n` matrix `board` containing `'X'` and `'O'`, **capture all regions that are 4-directionally surrounded by `'X'`**.

A region is captured by flipping all `'O'`s into `'X'`s in that surrounded region.

Notice that an `'O'` should **not** be flipped if it is on the border, or if it is connected (4-directionally) to an `'O'` that is on the border.

Modify `board` in place; you do not return anything.
questions.title: Surrounded Regions

questions.question:
Alice and Bob play a game on a tree of `n` nodes (labeled `1` to `n`) connected by `n − 1` edges. Alice secretly roots the tree at one node, chosen **uniformly at random** among all `n` nodes. Bob then makes `g` guesses; each guess is a pair `(u, v)` meaning Bob believes **`u` is the parent of `v`** in Alice's rooted tree.

Bob wins if **at least `k`** of his guesses are correct. Return the probability that Bob wins, as a reduced fraction `p/q`.
questions.title: The Story of a Tree
constraints: edges describe a connected tree (exactly n − 1 edges, no cycles)
0 ≤ g ≤ n − 1 guesses, each a directed pair (u, v)
The answer is a reduced fraction p/q (q > 0)

questions.question:
You are given `n` vertices labeled `0` to `n - 1` and a list of directed edges `edges[i] = [u, v]` meaning `u` must come before `v`.

Return **any valid topological ordering** of the vertices — a list in which, for every edge `u → v`, `u` appears before `v`. If no such ordering exists (the graph has a cycle), return an empty list `[]`.
questions.title: Topological Sort (Kahn's Algorithm)
constraints: edges are directed; edges[i] = [u, v] means u → v

questions.question:
A **transformation sequence** from word `beginWord` to word `endWord` using a dictionary `wordList` is a sequence of words `beginWord -> s₁ -> s₂ -> ... -> sₖ` such that:

- Every adjacent pair of words differs by a single letter.
- Every `sᵢ` for `1 ≤ i ≤ k` is in `wordList`. Note that `beginWord` does not need to be in `wordList`.
- `sₖ == endWord`.

Given two words `beginWord` and `endWord`, and a dictionary `wordList`, return *the **number of words** in the shortest transformation sequence from `beginWord` to `endWord`, or `0` if no such sequence exists.*
questions.title: Word Ladder
constraints: beginWord, endWord, and wordList[i] consist of lowercase English letters
All the words in wordList are unique

questions.question:
You are given `n` activities, each with a start time `start[i]` and a finish time `finish[i]`. A single resource can run only one activity at a time, so two activities are **compatible** only if they don't overlap.

Select the **maximum number** of mutually compatible activities — i.e. the largest subset whose intervals don't overlap. Return that count (and optionally the chosen activities).
questions.title: Activity Selection
constraints: An activity ending exactly when another begins is compatible (boundary touch allowed) — confirm with the interviewer
Times may be large; use long if you sum or subtract them

questions.question:
You are given two arrays, `A` and `B`, each containing `n` integers.

A pair of indices `(i, j)` is **beautiful** if `A[i] == B[j]`. A set of beautiful pairs is valid only if no index of `A` and no index of `B` is used more than once (a disjoint matching).

You must change **exactly one** element of `B` to any integer value. After making that single change, return the **maximum** possible number of beautiful pairs.
questions.title: Beautiful Pairs
constraints: Exactly one element of B must be changed (the change is mandatory, not optional)

questions.question:
You are given an array `ropes` of `n` positive lengths. You connect ropes one pair at a time; connecting two ropes of lengths `a` and `b` produces a single rope of length `a + b` and costs `a + b`.

The newly formed rope can be connected with other ropes in later steps. You must connect all ropes into a **single** rope.

Return the ***minimum total cost*** to connect every rope into one.
questions.title: Connect N Ropes with Minimum Cost
constraints: Total cost can exceed a 32-bit int (up to ~10⁹·log n) → accumulate in a long
If there is only one rope, the cost is 0 (nothing to connect)

questions.question:
You are given `n` items, where item `i` has a positive `value[i]` and a positive `weight[i]`, and a knapsack with capacity `W`.

Unlike the classic 0/1 version, you may take **fractions** of items: if you take a fraction `f` (with `0 ≤ f ≤ 1`) of item `i`, you use `f · weight[i]` of capacity and gain `f · value[i]` of value.

Return the ***maximum total value*** you can carry without exceeding the capacity `W`.
questions.title: Fractional Knapsack
constraints: Fractions of items are allowed; the answer may be a non-integer

questions.question:
There are `n` gas stations along a **circular** route, where the amount of gas at the `i`-th station is `gas[i]`.

You have a car with an unlimited gas tank, and it costs `cost[i]` of gas to travel from the `i`-th station to its next `(i + 1)`-th station. You begin the journey with an empty tank at one of the gas stations.

Given two integer arrays `gas` and `cost`, return *the starting gas station's index if you can travel around the circuit once in the clockwise direction, otherwise return* `-1`.

If there exists a solution, it is **guaranteed to be unique**.
questions.title: Gas Station
constraints: The answer is guaranteed to be unique if it exists

questions.question:
A group of `k` friends wants to buy `n` flowers from a florist. The original price of the `i`-th flower is `c[i]`.

The florist is greedy: the price a customer pays for a flower is `(1 + x) * c[i]`, where `x` is the number of flowers that **same customer** has **already purchased**. The first flower a customer buys costs `1 * c[i]`, the second `2 * c[i]`, and so on.

Every flower must be bought, and each flower is bought by exactly one of the `k` friends. Return the **minimum total cost** to buy all `n` flowers.
questions.title: Greedy Florist

questions.question:
Given a square grid of lowercase letters represented as `n` strings each of length `n` (more generally `n` rows of length `m`), determine whether the grid can be arranged so that **both** of the following hold:

1. Each **row** is sorted in non-decreasing (ascending) order, and
2. Each **column** is sorted in non-decreasing (top-to-bottom) order.

You may rearrange the characters **within each row** in any order, but you may not move characters between rows. Return `"YES"` if such an arrangement exists, otherwise `"NO"`.
questions.title: Grid Challenge
constraints: Each row has the same length m (1 ≤ m ≤ 100)
All characters are lowercase English letters 'a'–'z'

questions.question:
Alice has some number of cards and she wants to rearrange the cards into groups so that each group is of size `groupSize`, and consists of `groupSize` **consecutive** cards.

Given an integer array `hand` where `hand[i]` is the value written on the `i`-th card and an integer `groupSize`, return `true` if she can rearrange the cards, or `false` otherwise.
questions.title: Hand of Straights
constraints: Each group must be groupSize consecutive integers (e.g. [3,4,5])

questions.question:
You are given `n` symbols, each with a non-negative `frequency` (how often it appears). Construct a binary **prefix code** — a binary tree whose leaves are the symbols — that minimises the total number of encoded bits, where a symbol contributes `frequency × (its depth in the tree)` bits.

Return the ***minimum total encoded length*** (and/or the code assigned to each symbol). A prefix code means no symbol's codeword is a prefix of another's, which is guaranteed when every symbol is a leaf.
questions.title: Huffman Encoding
constraints: Total encoded length can exceed 32 bits → accumulate in a long
For n = 1 the single symbol is conventionally given a code of length 1 (one bit)

questions.question:
Jim runs a restaurant. There are `n` customers. Customer `i` (1-indexed) places an order at time `order[i]` and the dish takes `prep[i]` units of time to prepare, so it is **served at time `order[i] + prep[i]`**.

Server serves whichever dish finishes earliest. If two dishes finish at the same time, the customer with the **smaller id** is served first.

Return the **list of customer ids** in the order they are served.
questions.title: Jim and the Orders
constraints: Customer ids are 1..n; ties in serve time break by the smaller id

questions.question:
You are given `n` jobs. Each job `i` has a **deadline** `deadline[i]` and a **profit** `profit[i]`, and takes exactly **one unit of time** to run. A single machine runs one job per time unit, starting at time 1.

A job earns its profit only if it is scheduled to finish at or before its deadline. Choose a subset and an ordering that **maximises the total profit** of on-time jobs. Return the number of jobs done and the total profit (or just the maximum profit).
questions.title: Job Sequencing with Deadlines
constraints: 1 ≤ deadline[i] ≤ n (a deadline beyond n is never more useful than n)
1 ≤ profit[i] ≤ 10⁹ (sum can exceed a 32-bit int → accumulate profit in a long)
Each job is unit time and can be dropped if it can't be scheduled on time

questions.question:
You are given a 0-indexed array of integers `nums` of length `n`. You are initially positioned at `nums[0]`.

Each element `nums[i]` represents the maximum length of a forward jump from index `i`. In other words, if you are at `nums[i]`, you can jump to any `nums[i + j]` where `0 <= j <= nums[i]` and `i + j < n`.

Return *the minimum number of jumps to reach* `nums[n - 1]`. The test cases are generated such that you can reach `nums[n - 1]`.
questions.title: Jump Game II
constraints: It is guaranteed you can reach the last index
From index i you may jump to any index in [i+1, i+nums[i]]

questions.question:
You are given an integer array `nums`. You are initially positioned at the array's **first index**, and each element in the array represents your **maximum jump length** at that position.

Return `true` if you can reach the ***last index***, or `false` otherwise.
questions.title: Jump Game
constraints: From index i you may jump to any index in [i+1, i+nums[i]]

questions.question:
You are given a permutation of the integers `1` to `n` and a number `k`. You may perform **at most `k` swaps** of any two elements.

Return the **lexicographically largest** permutation obtainable with at most `k` swaps.
questions.title: Largest Permutation
constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ 10⁹  (effectively capped at n − 1 useful swaps)
The input is a permutation of 1..n (each value 1..n appears exactly once)

questions.question:
Lena is preparing for an important coding contest by competing in `n` preliminary contests. Each contest `i` has a luck amount `L[i]` and an importance flag `T[i]` (1 = important, 0 = unimportant).

If Lena **wins** a contest, her luck balance **decreases** by `L[i]`. If she **loses**, her luck balance **increases** by `L[i]`.

She wants to **maximise** her luck balance but can **lose at most `k`** of the important contests. She may lose any number of unimportant contests. Return the maximum luck balance she can achieve.
questions.title: Luck Balance

questions.question:
Mark wants to buy toys for his son's birthday. Given the `prices` of toys in the shop and the amount `k` of dollars Mark has, determine the **maximum number of toys** Mark can buy.

Each toy can be bought at most once, and Mark cannot spend more than `k` dollars in total.
questions.title: Mark and Toys
constraints: Mark may buy any subset; he wants the largest possible subset by count

questions.question:
Given an array of integers `arr` and a number `k`, you must create an array of length `k` from elements of `arr` such that its **unfairness** is minimised.

The **unfairness** of an array is defined as `max(array) − min(array)`. Return the minimum possible unfairness over all length-`k` subsets of `arr`.
questions.title: Max Min

questions.question:
A triplet is an array of three integers. You are given a 2D integer array `triplets`, where `triplets[i] = [aᵢ, bᵢ, cᵢ]` describes the `i`-th triplet. You are also given an integer array `target = [x, y, z]` that describes the triplet you want to obtain.

To obtain `target`, you may apply the following operation any number of times:

- Choose two indices (0-indexed) `i` and `j` (`i != j`) and **update** `triplets[j]` to become `[max(aᵢ, aⱼ), max(bᵢ, bⱼ), max(cᵢ, cⱼ)]`.

Return `true` *if it is possible to obtain the* `target` *triplet* `[x, y, z]` *as an element of* `triplets`, *or* `false` *otherwise.*
questions.title: Merge Triplets to Form Target Triplet
constraints: 1 ≤ aᵢ, bᵢ, cᵢ, x, y, z ≤ 1000
Merging replaces a triplet with the component-wise max of two triplets

questions.question:
You are given two arrays, `arr` and `dep`, of size `n`, where `arr[i]` and `dep[i]` are the arrival and departure times of the `i`-th train at a station (with `arr[i] ≤ dep[i]`). A platform can hold at most one train at a time, and a train occupies a platform for the whole closed interval `[arr[i], dep[i]]`.

Return the ***minimum number of platforms*** needed so that no train ever waits. By convention, if one train departs at the exact moment another arrives, they ***cannot*** share a platform.
questions.title: Minimum Number of Platforms
constraints: Times are given in a comparable format (e.g. integers like 900 for 09:00, or minutes since midnight)
A train arriving exactly when another departs needs its own platform (arrival-first tie rule)

questions.question:
You are given two arrays `A` and `B`, each of `n` integers, and an integer `k`.

You may **permute** the elements of both arrays in any order. Determine whether there exists a permutation such that for **every** index `i`, `A[i] + B[i] >= k`.

Return `"YES"` if such a permutation exists, otherwise `"NO"`.
questions.title: Permuting Two Arrays
constraints: Both arrays have the same length n

questions.question:
Priyanka must distribute `n` toys into containers. Each toy `i` has a weight `w[i]`. A single container can hold any number of toys, as long as the **difference between the maximum and minimum weight** of the toys it holds is **at most 4** — i.e. all its toys fit in some window `[base, base + 4]`.

Return the **minimum number of containers** needed to hold all the toys.
questions.title: Priyanka and Toys
constraints: A container holds toys whose weights span at most 4 units (inclusive)

questions.question:
A **Decent Number** has the following properties:

1. It contains only the digits `3` and `5`.
2. The number of `5`s in it is divisible by `3`.
3. The number of `3`s in it is divisible by `5`.

Given the length `n`, find the **largest** decent number of exactly `n` digits. If no such number exists, print `-1`.
questions.title: Sherlock and the Beast
constraints: The answer can be a very large number — build it as a string, never an integer
Multiple test cases may be given; solve each independently

questions.question:
You are given two integer arrays `nums1` and `nums2` sorted in **non-decreasing order** and an integer `k`.

Define a pair `(u, v)` which consists of one element from the first array and one element from the second array.

Return *the* `k` *pairs* `(u₁, v₁), (u₂, v₂), ..., (uₖ, vₖ)` *with the smallest sums*.
questions.title: Find K Pairs with Smallest Sums
constraints: nums1 and nums2 both sorted in non-decreasing order

questions.question:
The **median** is the middle value in an ordered list. If the list has an even number of elements, the median is the mean of the two middle values.

Implement the `MedianFinder` class:
- `MedianFinder()` initialises the object.
- `void addNum(int num)` adds the integer `num` from the data stream to the data structure.
- `double findMedian()` returns the median of all elements so far. Answers within 10⁻⁵ of the actual answer are accepted.
questions.title: Find Median from Data Stream
constraints: There will be at least one element before findMedian is called
At most 5 × 10⁴ calls to addNum and findMedian
Follow-up: if all numbers are in [0, 100], can you optimise? What if 99% are in [0, 100]?

questions.question:
Suppose LeetCode will start its **IPO** soon. To attract investors, it wants to do some projects to maximize its capital before the IPO. Since it has limited resources, it can finish at most `k` distinct projects before the IPO.

You are given `n` projects where the `i`-th project has a pure profit `profits[i]` and a minimum capital `capital[i]` needed to start it.

Initially, you have `w` capital. When you finish a project, you obtain its pure profit and that profit is **added** to your total capital.

Pick a list of **at most** `k` distinct projects to maximize your final capital, and return *the final maximized capital*.
questions.title: IPO

questions.question:
Given an array `points` where `points[i] = [xᵢ, yᵢ]` represents a point on the X-Y plane and an integer `k`, return the `k` closest points to the origin `(0, 0)`.

The distance between two points is the Euclidean distance: √((x₁−x₂)² + (y₁−y₂)²). You may return the answer in **any order**. The answer is guaranteed to be unique (except for the order).
questions.title: K Closest Points to Origin
constraints: The answer is unique up to ordering

questions.question:
Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return *the* `kᵗʰ` *largest element in the array*.

Note that it is the `kᵗʰ` largest element in the **sorted order**, not the `kᵗʰ` distinct element.

Can you solve it without sorting?
questions.title: Kth Largest Element in an Array

questions.question:
Numbers arrive one at a time. After reading each number, print the median of all numbers seen so far.

If the count of numbers seen is odd, the median is the middle element of the sorted sequence. If it is even, the median is the average of the two middle elements.

Print each median on its own line, formatted to one decimal place.
questions.title: Find the Running Median
constraints: Print each running median to exactly one decimal place
Median of an even count is the average of the two middle values (may end in .5)

questions.question:
Given a characters array `tasks`, representing the tasks a CPU needs to do, where each letter represents a different task. Tasks could be done in any order. Each task takes one unit of time. For each unit of time, the CPU could complete either one task or be idle.

However, there is a non-negative integer `n` that represents the **cooldown** period between two **same tasks** (the same letter): there must be at least `n` units of time between any two same tasks.

Return the **least number of intervals** the CPU will take to finish all the given tasks.
questions.title: Task Scheduler
constraints: tasks[i] is an uppercase English letter (only 26 distinct types)

questions.question: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return **the `k` most frequent elements**. You may return the answer in any order.
questions.title: Top K Frequent Elements
constraints: k is in the range [1, number of unique elements in nums]
The answer is guaranteed to be unique
Follow-up: your algorithm's time complexity must be better than O(n log n)

questions.question:
You are given an array of non-overlapping intervals `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [startᵢ, endᵢ]` represent the start and end of the iᵗʰ interval, and `intervals` is **sorted in ascending order by startᵢ**.

You are also given an interval `newInterval = [start, end]` that represents the start and end of another interval.

Insert `newInterval` into `intervals` such that `intervals` is still sorted in ascending order by `startᵢ` and `intervals` still does not have any overlapping intervals (merge overlapping intervals if necessary).

Return `intervals` **after the insertion**.
questions.title: Insert Interval
constraints: intervals is sorted by startᵢ in ascending order

questions.question:
Given an array of meeting time intervals `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [startᵢ, endᵢ]`, return the **minimum number of conference rooms required** so that all meetings can be held.

A room can be reused once a meeting finishes: a meeting ending at time `t` frees its room for another meeting starting at time `t` (back-to-back is allowed).
questions.title: Meeting Rooms II
constraints: A room can be reused starting exactly at the time the previous meeting ended

questions.question:
Given an array of meeting time `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [startᵢ, endᵢ]`, determine if a person could **attend all meetings**.

A person can attend all meetings if and only if **no two meetings overlap**. Meetings that merely touch — one ending exactly when the next begins, like `[0,30]` and `[30,60]` — do **not** conflict.
questions.title: Meeting Rooms
constraints: A meeting ending at time t and another starting at t do NOT overlap

questions.question:
Given an array of `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [startᵢ, endᵢ]`, **merge all overlapping intervals**, and return an array of the non-overlapping intervals that cover all the intervals in the input.

Two intervals overlap if they share any point, including a single shared endpoint — so `[1,4]` and `[4,5]` merge into `[1,5]`.
questions.title: Merge Intervals
constraints: The returned list must be sorted and non-overlapping

questions.question:
There are some spherical balloons taped onto a flat wall that represents the XY-plane. The balloons are represented as a 2D integer array `points` where `points[i] = [x_start, x_end]` denotes a balloon whose **horizontal diameter** stretches between `x_start` and `x_end`. You do not know the exact y-coordinates of the balloons.

Arrows can be shot up **directly vertically** (in the positive y-direction) from different points along the x-axis. A balloon with `x_start` and `x_end` is **burst** by an arrow shot at `x` if `x_start <= x <= x_end`. There is no limit to the number of arrows that can be shot. A shot arrow keeps traveling up infinitely, bursting any balloons in its path.

Given the array `points`, return *the **minimum** number of arrows that must be shot to burst all balloons*.
questions.title: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons

questions.question:
Given an array of `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [startᵢ, endᵢ]`, return the **minimum number of intervals you need to remove** to make the rest of the intervals non-overlapping.

Intervals that only touch at a point, like `[1,2]` and `[2,3]`, are considered **non-overlapping** — you do not need to remove either.
questions.title: Non-overlapping Intervals
constraints: An interval always has start < end (no zero-length intervals)

questions.question:
You are given a **sorted unique** integer array `nums`.

A *range* `[a,b]` is the set of all integers from `a` to `b` (inclusive).

Return the **smallest sorted** list of ranges that **cover all the numbers in the array exactly**. That is, each element of `nums` is covered by exactly one of the ranges, and there is no integer `x` such that `x` is in one of the ranges but not in `nums`.

Each range `[a,b]` in the list should be output as:

- `"a->b"` if `a != b`
- `"a"` if `a == b`
questions.title: Summary Ranges
constraints: All the values of nums are unique
nums is sorted in ascending order

questions.question:
You are given two **non-empty** linked lists representing two non-negative integers. The digits are stored in ***reverse order***, and each node contains a single digit. Add the two numbers and return the sum as a linked list.

You may assume the two numbers do not contain any leading zero, except the number 0 itself.

Because the digits are reversed, the head of each list is the least-significant (ones) digit — which is exactly the digit you add first.
questions.title: Add Two Numbers
constraints: The number of nodes in each list is in the range [1, 100]
Each number is guaranteed to have no leading zeros, except the number 0 itself
The two lists may have different lengths

questions.question:
You are given the heads of two singly linked lists, `headA` and `headB`.

Return `1` if the two lists are **identical** — the same number of nodes and the same `val` at every position, in order — and `0` otherwise.
questions.title: Compare Two Linked Lists
constraints: The lists are singly linked (next pointers only)
Comparison is by value and length, not by node identity

questions.question:
A linked list of length n is given such that each node contains an additional random pointer, which could point to any node in the list, or `null`.

Construct a **deep copy** of the list. The deep copy should consist of exactly n brand-new nodes, where each new node's value is set to the value of its corresponding original node. Both the next and random pointers of the new nodes should point to new nodes in the copied list such that the pointers in the original and copied list represent the same list state. None of the pointers in the new list should point to nodes in the original list.

Return the head of the copied linked list.
questions.title: Copy List with Random Pointer
constraints: Node.random is null or points to some node in the list
The new list must be completely independent of the original

questions.question:
You are given the `head` of a singly linked list and an integer `position` (0-based).

Delete the node at index `position` and return *the head of the modified list*.

You may assume `0 ≤ position < length`, so a node always exists at that index.
questions.title: Delete a Node at a Given Position in a Linked List
constraints: The list is singly linked (next pointers only)

questions.question:
Given `head`, the head of a linked list, determine if the linked list has a cycle in it.

There is a cycle if some node can be reached again by continuously following the `next` pointer. Return `true` if there is a cycle, otherwise return `false`. You should not modify the list.
questions.title: Linked List Cycle Detection
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 10⁴]
The cycle, if present, is created by the tail's next pointing to an earlier node (or to itself)

questions.question:
You are given the heads of two singly linked lists, `headA` and `headB`. The two lists may **merge** at some node — after which they share all subsequent nodes (a Y-shape).

Return *the node at which the two lists intersect*. If they do not intersect, return `null`.

Intersection is by node **identity**, not value. The lists are acyclic and must not be modified.
questions.title: Find the Merge Point of Two Linked Lists

examples.input: A = [4, 1, 8, 4, 5], B = [5, 6, 1, 8, 4, 5], merge at node with val 8

constraints: If the lists intersect, they share a common suffix (no diverging after the merge)
The lists are acyclic; do not modify them

questions.question:
You are given the `head` of a singly linked list and an integer `data`.

Create a **new node** holding `data` and insert it at the **front** of the list, so it becomes the new head. Return *the head of the modified list*.
questions.title: Insert a Node at the Head of a Linked List
constraints: The list is singly linked (next pointers only)
Insertion must run in O(1) time

questions.question:
You are given the `head` of a singly linked list, an integer `data`, and an integer `position` (0-based).

Insert a **new node** holding `data` so that it ends up at index `position` in the list. Return *the head of the modified list*.

You may assume `0 ≤ position ≤ length`, so inserting at `position == length` appends to the end.
questions.title: Insert a Node at a Specific Position in a Linked List
constraints: The list is singly linked (next pointers only)

questions.question:
You are given the `head` of a singly linked list and an integer `data`.

Create a **new node** holding `data` and insert it at the **end** of the list, so it becomes the new tail. Return *the head of the modified list*.

If the list is empty, the new node becomes the head.
questions.title: Insert a Node at the Tail of a Linked List
constraints: The list is singly linked (next pointers only)
Without a tail pointer, the append is O(n)

questions.question:
You are given the `head` of a singly linked list. A **cycle** exists if some node's `next` points back to an earlier node, so following `next` repeats forever.

Return `true` if the list contains a cycle, and `false` otherwise. Do not modify the list.
questions.title: Detect a Cycle in a Linked List
constraints: The cycle, if present, can start at any node (including the head)
Must run in O(1) extra space for the optimal solution

questions.question:
Design a data structure that follows the constraints of a **Least Recently Used (LRU) cache**.

Implement the `LRUCache` class:

- `LRUCache(int capacity)` initializes the cache with positive size `capacity`.
- `int get(int key)` returns the value of the key if it exists, otherwise returns `-1`.
- `void put(int key, int value)` updates the value if the key exists; otherwise adds the key-value pair. If inserting causes the number of keys to exceed `capacity`, evict the **least recently used** key.

The functions `get` and `put` must each run in `O(1)` average time complexity.
questions.title: LRU Cache

examples.input: LRUCache(2); put(1,1); put(2,2); get(1); put(3,3); get(2); put(4,4); get(1); get(3); get(4)

constraints: At most 2 × 10⁵ calls to get and put
Both get and put must be O(1) average time

questions.question:
You are given an array of `k` linked lists `lists`, where each list is sorted in ascending order.

*Merge all the lists into one sorted linked list and return its head.*

The result must itself be sorted in ascending order, and it should be built from the existing nodes (you may relink them).
questions.title: Merge k Sorted Lists
constraints: Each lists[i] is sorted in ascending order
The sum of lists[i].length will not exceed 10⁴ (this is N)

questions.question:
You are given the heads of two sorted singly linked lists, `list1` and `list2`, each sorted in non-decreasing order.

Merge them into one **sorted** list by splicing together the existing nodes, and return *the head of the merged list*.
questions.title: Merge Two Sorted Linked Lists
constraints: Both list1 and list2 are sorted in non-decreasing order
Either or both lists may be empty

questions.question:
You are given the heads of two sorted linked lists `list1` and `list2`.

Merge the two lists into one **sorted** list. The list should be made by splicing together the nodes of the first two lists. Return *the head of the merged linked list*.
questions.title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
constraints: The number of nodes in both lists is in the range [0, 50]
Both list1 and list2 are sorted in non-decreasing order

questions.question:
Given the `head` of a singly linked list, return *the middle node* of the linked list.

If there are **two middle nodes** (the list has an even number of nodes), return the **second** middle node.

For example, for `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]` the two middles are `3` and `4`, and you must return the node `4`.
questions.title: Middle of the Linked List
constraints: The number of nodes in the list is in the range [1, 100]
The list is non-empty (at least one node)

questions.question:
Given the `head` of a singly linked list, return `true` if it is a *palindrome* or `false` otherwise.

A list is a palindrome when the sequence of node values reads the same forwards and backwards.

**Follow-up:** Could you do it in `O(n)` time and `O(1)` extra space?
questions.title: Palindrome Linked List
constraints: The number of nodes in the list is in the range [1, 10⁵]
A single node and an empty list are considered palindromes

questions.question:
You are given the `head` of a singly linked list.

Print each element's value on its own line, in order from the head to the tail. If the list is empty, print nothing.

Return nothing — this is a side-effect (printing) task.
questions.title: Print the Elements of a Linked List
constraints: The list is singly linked (next pointers only)

questions.question:
Given the `head` of a linked list, remove the `n`-th node from the end of the list and return its head.

Follow up: Could you do this in one pass?
questions.title: Remove Nth Node From End of List
constraints: The number of nodes in the list is sz

questions.question:
You are given the head of a singly linked list. The list can be represented as:

L0 → L1 → … → Ln-1 → Ln

Reorder the list to be in the following form:

L0 → Ln → L1 → Ln-1 → L2 → Ln-2 → …

You may not modify the values in the list's nodes. Only the nodes themselves may be changed.
questions.title: Reorder List
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 5 × 10⁴]
You must reorder by relinking nodes, not by swapping values

questions.question:
You are given the `head` of a **doubly linked list**, where each node has a `val`, a `next` pointer, and a `prev` pointer.

Reverse the list in place by re-pointing each node's links, and return *the head of the reversed list*.

Do not allocate new nodes — rewire the existing ones.
questions.title: Reverse a Doubly Linked List
constraints: Each node has both next and prev pointers (prev of head is null, next of tail is null)
Must run in O(1) extra space

questions.question:
You are given the `head` of a singly linked list.

Reverse the list so the last node becomes the first, and return **the head of the reversed list**.

The reversal should be done in place — rewire the existing nodes rather than allocating new ones.
questions.title: Reverse a Linked List
constraints: The list is singly linked (next pointers only)

questions.question:
Given the `head` of a singly linked list and two integers `left` and `right` where `left <= right`, reverse the nodes of the list from position `left` to position `right`, and return *the reversed list*.

Positions are 1-indexed: the head is position 1. The reversal is over the **inclusive** range `[left, right]`.
questions.title: Reverse Linked List II
constraints: The number of nodes in the list is n
Follow up: can you do it in one pass?

questions.question:
Given the `head` of a singly linked list, reverse the list, and return *the reversed list's head*.

Each node holds an integer `val` and a `next` pointer. After reversing, the node that was last should be the head, and the original head should point to `null`.
questions.title: Reverse Linked List
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 5000]
Follow up: can you do it both iteratively and recursively?

questions.question:
Given the `head` of a linked list, reverse the nodes of the list `k` at a time, and return *the modified list*.

`k` is a positive integer and is less than or equal to the length of the linked list. If the number of nodes is not a multiple of `k` then **left-out nodes, in the end, should remain as they are**.

You may not alter the values in the list's nodes, only nodes themselves may be changed.
questions.title: Reverse Nodes in k-Group
constraints: The number of nodes in the list is n
Follow-up: Can you solve the problem in O(1) extra memory space?

questions.question:
Given the `head` of a linked list, return *the list after sorting it in **ascending order***.

The follow-up: can you sort the list in `O(n log n)` time and `O(1)` memory (i.e. constant space)?
questions.title: Sort List
constraints: The number of nodes in the list is in the range [0, 5 × 10⁴]

questions.question:
An Armstrong number (a.k.a. narcissistic number) of `k` digits is a number equal to the sum of its own digits each raised to the power `k`.

For example `153 = 1³ + 5³ + 3³`. Given `n`, return whether it is an Armstrong number.
questions.title: Armstrong Number
constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 2³¹ − 1 (use a 64-bit accumulator for the power sum)
k is the number of digits in n

questions.question:
Compute the nth **Catalan number** `Cₙ`.

The Catalan numbers begin `1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, 132, …` and count, among many things: the number of distinct binary search trees with `n` nodes, the number of valid sequences of `n` pairs of balanced parentheses, and the number of triangulations of a convex `(n + 2)`-gon.

Return `Cₙ` exactly (for small `n`) or modulo a given prime `p` (for large `n`).
questions.title: Catalan Numbers
constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 10⁶ when working modulo a prime p
0 ≤ n ≤ 33 if returning an exact 64-bit value (C₃₅ overflows a signed 64-bit integer)
p is prime and p > 2n when using the closed form mod p (so inverses exist)

questions.question:
Given `k` congruences

`x ≡ a₁ (mod m₁)`, `x ≡ a₂ (mod m₂)`, …, `x ≡ a_k (mod m_k)`,

where the moduli `m₁, …, m_k` are **pairwise coprime**, find the unique `x` in `[0, M)` satisfying all of them, where `M = m₁·m₂·…·m_k`. The Chinese Remainder Theorem guarantees exactly one such `x` exists.
questions.title: Chinese Remainder Theorem
constraints: 1 ≤ mᵢ, and the mᵢ are pairwise coprime (gcd(mᵢ, mⱼ) = 1 for i ≠ j)
M = ∏ mᵢ can be enormous — use big integers (Python) or mulmod with long / 128-bit intermediates (Java)
Return the unique solution normalised to [0, M)

questions.question:
The Collatz process starts from a positive integer `n` and repeatedly applies: if `n` is even, replace it with `n / 2`; if `n` is odd, replace it with `3n + 1`. The conjecture (unproven) says this always reaches `1`.

Given `n`, return the number of steps to reach `1`. (By convention, `n = 1` takes `0` steps.)
questions.title: Collatz Sequence Length
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁶ (or larger; intermediate values can far exceed n)
Intermediate values may exceed 2³¹ — use a 64-bit integer

questions.question:
Marie invented a calendar where the Day of the Programmer falls on the **256th day** of the year. Given a year `year` in the inclusive range 1700 to 2700, return the date of the 256th day in the format `dd.mm.yyyy`.

The country used the **Julian** calendar through 1917, then switched to the **Gregorian** calendar. The transition happened in **1918**, when the day after January 31 was February 14 — that year February had only 15 days.
questions.title: Day of the Programmer
constraints: Julian leap year (year ≤ 1917): year divisible by 4
Gregorian leap year (year ≥ 1919): divisible by 400, or divisible by 4 and not by 100
1918 is the transition year: February has 15 days
Output format is exactly dd.mm.yyyy with zero-padding

questions.question:
A teacher asks a student to find a specific page `p` in a textbook that has `n` pages. The student can turn sheets from the **front** of the book or from the **back**, whichever is closer.

Each sheet has two pages: page 1 is on the first sheet by itself, then pages 2 and 3 share a sheet, pages 4 and 5 share a sheet, and so on.

Given `n` and `p`, return the **minimum number of sheet turns** needed to arrive at page `p`.
questions.title: Drawing Book
constraints: Each sheet holds exactly two page numbers (except the cover behaviour described)
Turning is counted in whole sheets, never half a sheet

questions.question:
**Euler's totient function** φ(n) counts the integers k in the range [1, n] for which gcd(k, n) = 1 (i.e. k is coprime to n).

Solve two versions:

1. **Single value**: given n, return φ(n).
2. **All values up to N**: return an array `phi[0..N]` where `phi[i] = φ(i)` for every i.

Use the prime-factorisation product formula φ(n) = n · ∏_{p | n} (1 − 1/p), where the product runs over the *distinct* primes dividing n.
questions.title: Euler's Totient Function
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁹ for the single-value version (O(√n) factorisation)
1 ≤ N ≤ 10⁷ for the sieve version (O(N) memory)
All results are positive integers, φ(n) ≤ n

questions.question:
Given two integers `a` and `b`, return a triple `(g, x, y)` where `g = gcd(a, b)` and `x, y` are integers satisfying the **Bézout identity**:

`a·x + b·y = g`.

As the headline application, given `a` and a modulus `m` with `gcd(a, m) = 1`, return the **modular inverse** `a⁻¹ mod m` — the unique value in `[0, m)` such that `a · a⁻¹ ≡ 1 (mod m)`.
questions.title: Extended Euclidean Algorithm
constraints: −10⁹ ≤ a, b ≤ 10⁹ (use 64-bit integers in Java for the coefficients)
For the inverse: 1 ≤ a < m, with gcd(a, m) = 1 (otherwise no inverse exists)
1 ≤ m ≤ 10⁹ (m need NOT be prime — that's the point)
Return x, y as integers; the inverse must be normalised to [0, m)

questions.question:
Given a non-negative integer `n`, return `n!` (n factorial), the product of all positive integers from `1` to `n`.

By definition `0! = 1`. For example, `5! = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120`.

Discuss what happens to the return type as `n` grows.
questions.title: Factorial of a Number
constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 20 if the answer must fit in a signed 64-bit integer
n is an integer; negative inputs are invalid

questions.question:
Given an integer `n`, return the number of **trailing zeroes** in `n!`.

Note that `n! = n × (n − 1) × (n − 2) × … × 3 × 2 × 1`.

**Follow-up:** Could you write a solution that works in logarithmic time complexity?
questions.title: Factorial Trailing Zeroes
constraints: n! is astronomically large — you must NOT compute it directly

questions.question:
Given two polynomials `A(x) = Σ aᵢxⁱ` and `B(x) = Σ bⱼxʲ` (equivalently, two large integers written as digit arrays), compute their product `C(x) = A(x)·B(x)`.

The product's coefficients are the **convolution** `cₖ = Σ_{i+j=k} aᵢ·bⱼ`. With `lenA + lenB − 1` output coefficients, the schoolbook method is `O(n²)`; you are asked to do it in `O(n log n)` using the Fast Fourier Transform.
questions.title: FFT Polynomial Multiplication
constraints: 1 ≤ lenA, lenB ≤ 2·10⁵ (so O(n²) ≈ 4·10¹⁰ is too slow; O(n log n) is required)
Coefficients fit in 32-bit integers; products accumulate, so the result needs 64-bit / careful precision
Use complex doubles for FFT, or a prime modulus for an exact NTT
Output length is lenA + lenB − 1; pad working arrays to the next power of two

questions.question:
The board is an `m x n` grid of cells, each either live (`1`) or dead (`0`). Each cell interacts with its eight neighbors (horizontal, vertical, diagonal) using the following rules (applied ***simultaneously*** to every cell):

1. Any live cell with fewer than two live neighbors dies (under-population).
2. Any live cell with two or three live neighbors lives on.
3. Any live cell with more than three live neighbors dies (over-population).
4. Any dead cell with exactly three live neighbors becomes a live cell (reproduction).

The next state is created by applying the above rules simultaneously to every cell in the current state. Given the current state of the `board`, update it **in place** to reflect its next state.

***Follow-up:*** Could you solve it in place? Remember the board needs to be updated simultaneously. And what about the board being infinite?
questions.title: Game of Life

questions.question:
Given two non-negative integers `a` and `b`, compute:

1. Their **greatest common divisor** `gcd(a, b)` — the largest integer that divides both.
2. Their **least common multiple** `lcm(a, b)` — the smallest positive integer that both divide.

Return both. Use the relationship `a * b = gcd(a, b) * lcm(a, b)`, rearranged carefully to avoid integer overflow.
questions.title: GCD and LCM
constraints: 0 ≤ a, b ≤ 10⁹ (so a*b can reach 10¹⁸ — overflow-aware ordering matters)
gcd(x, 0) = x and gcd(0, 0) = 0 by convention
lcm is 0 if either input is 0

questions.question:
Given two non-negative integers `a` and `b`, return their greatest common divisor (GCD) — the largest integer that divides both without a remainder.

By convention `gcd(a, 0) = a`. Aim for better than trial division.
questions.title: GCD of Two Numbers
constraints: 0 ≤ a, b ≤ 10⁹ (or up to Long range)
At least one of a, b is positive for a meaningful answer
If negatives are allowed, operate on |a| and |b|

questions.question:
At the annual meeting of Board of Directors of a company, every two directors shake hands **exactly once**. Given the number of directors `n`, determine the **total number of handshakes** that take place.

For each of `t` test cases, you are given an integer `n` and must output the handshake count.
questions.title: Handshake
constraints: Each pair shakes hands exactly once
Order does not matter (A↔B is a single handshake)
The answer can exceed a 32-bit integer for large n

questions.question:
Write an algorithm to determine if a number `n` is **happy**.

A **happy number** is a number defined by the following process:

- Starting with any positive integer, replace the number by the **sum of the squares of its digits**.
- Repeat the process until the number **equals 1** (where it will stay), or it **loops endlessly in a cycle** that does not include 1.
- Those numbers for which this process **ends in 1** are happy.

Return `true` if `n` is a happy number, and `false` if not.
questions.title: Happy Number

questions.question:
Given integers `n` and `r` and a **prime** `p`, compute the binomial coefficient `C(n, r) mod p`.

The twist versus the standard problem: `n` may be **much larger than `p`** (for example `n` up to `10¹⁸` with `p` a small prime like `13` or `1000003`). The usual 'precompute factorials up to n' approach is impossible (n is too large) and incorrect (factorials contain factors of p). Use Lucas' theorem.
questions.title: Lucas' Theorem
constraints: 0 ≤ r ≤ n ≤ 10¹⁸ (n can vastly exceed p)
p is prime and 2 ≤ p ≤ 10⁶ or so (small enough to precompute factorials up to p−1)
Define C(n, r) = 0 when r > n
Use long in Java for digit products; Python big ints are exact

questions.question:
Compute the nth **Fibonacci number** `Fₙ`, where `F₀ = 0`, `F₁ = 1`, and `Fₙ = Fₙ₋₁ + Fₙ₋₂` for `n ≥ 2`.

`n` can be as large as `10¹⁸`, so an O(n) loop is far too slow. Return `Fₙ` modulo a given modulus `p` (Fibonacci numbers grow exponentially, so for large n the answer is always requested mod p).
questions.title: Matrix Exponentiation (Fibonacci)
constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 10¹⁸ (use 64-bit for n; O(log n) ≈ 60 matrix multiplies)
Answers are taken mod p with 1 ≤ p ≤ 10⁹ + 7; reduce after every multiply
Entry products of two sub-p values reach ~10¹⁸ → use long in Java

questions.question: Given an array of `points` where `points[i] = [xi, yi]` represents a point on the X-Y plane, return *the maximum number of points that lie on the same straight line*.
questions.title: Max Points on a Line

questions.question:
Given non-negative integers `base`, `exp`, and a positive integer `m`, compute `(base^exp) mod m`.

`exp` can be very large (up to 10¹⁸), so you cannot compute `base^exp` and then take the modulus — the intermediate value would have billions of digits. You must combine the exponentiation with the modular reduction.

This is the engine behind LeetCode 50 (*Pow(x, n)*, the non-modular real-number twin) and LeetCode 372 (*Super Pow*).
questions.title: Modular Exponentiation
constraints: 1 ≤ m ≤ 10⁹ (so operands fit and long products stay below 2⁶³)

questions.question:
Given integers `n`, `r`, and a **prime** modulus `p` with `p > n`, compute the binomial coefficient

`C(n, r) = n! / (r! · (n − r)!)`  taken modulo `p`.

You will answer **many** such queries against the same `p` (commonly `p = 1\,000\,000\,007`). Preprocess once so each query is `O(1)`. Define `C(n, r) = 0` when `r < 0` or `r > n`.
questions.title: nCr mod p
constraints: 0 ≤ r ≤ n ≤ 10⁶ (precompute factorial tables of this size)
p is prime and p > n (so Fermat's inverse applies and no factor of p appears in n!)
p ≤ 10⁹ + 7 (typical), products fit in 64-bit after each mod
Many queries → O(n) precompute, O(1) per query is required
Return 0 for r < 0 or r > n

questions.question:
Return the `n`-th Fibonacci number, where `F(0) = 0`, `F(1) = 1`, and `F(n) = F(n−1) + F(n−2)` for `n ≥ 2`.

Discuss how your approach scales as `n` grows and what happens to the return type.
questions.title: Nth Fibonacci Number
constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 92 if the answer must fit in a signed 64-bit integer
0 ≤ n ≤ 10⁶ or beyond with BigInteger / arbitrary precision

questions.question:
Two kangaroos are on a number line at positions `x1` and `x2`. The first kangaroo moves `v1` units per jump; the second moves `v2` units per jump. Both jump at the same time, the same number of times.

Return `"YES"` if there is some number of jumps after which both kangaroos are at the **same location**, otherwise return `"NO"`.

Assume the first kangaroo starts at or behind the second (`x1 < x2`).
questions.title: Number Line Jumps
constraints: The number of jumps must be a whole, non-negative number

questions.question:
Given an integer `x`, return `true` if `x` is a palindrome, and `false` otherwise.

An integer is a **palindrome** when it reads the same backward as forward.

For example, `121` is a palindrome while `123` is not.

**Follow-up:** Could you solve it without converting the integer to a string?
questions.title: Palindrome Number
constraints: x fits in a 32-bit signed integer
No string conversion in the follow-up variant

questions.question:
You are given a **large integer** represented as an integer array `digits`, where each `digits[i]` is the `iᵗʰ` digit of the integer. The digits are ordered from **most significant to least significant** in left-to-right order. The large integer does not contain any leading 0's.

Increment the large integer by one and return the resulting array of digits.
questions.title: Plus One
constraints: digits does not contain any leading 0's

questions.question:
Implement `pow(x, n)`, which calculates `x` raised to the power `n` (i.e., `xⁿ`).

`x` is a floating-point number and `n` is a signed 32-bit integer that may be **negative**.
questions.title: Pow(x, n)
constraints: n is an integer; either x is not zero or n > 0

questions.question:
The **super digit** of an integer is defined recursively: if it has only one digit, that's the super digit; otherwise it is the super digit of the sum of its digits.

You are given a string `n` and an integer `k`. The number `p` is formed by **concatenating the string `n` exactly `k` times**. Return the super digit of `p`.

For example, if `n = "148"` and `k = 3`, then `p = "148148148"`. The super digit reduces `148148148 → 1+4+8+1+4+8+1+4+8 = 39 → 3+9 = 12 → 1+2 = 3`, so the answer is **3**.
questions.title: Recursive Digit Sum
constraints: 1 ≤ |n| ≤ 10⁵ (n is given as a string of digits)
p (n repeated k times) can be astronomically large — never build it
The answer is a single digit 0–9

questions.question:
You are given an `n x n` 2D `matrix` representing an image. Rotate the image by **90 degrees (clockwise)**.

You have to rotate the image ***in place***, which means you have to modify the input 2D matrix directly. **Do not** allocate another 2D matrix and do the rotation.
questions.title: Rotate Image
constraints: Rotation must be performed in place

questions.question:
Given two integers `L` and `R` (with `L ≤ R`), return all prime numbers in the inclusive range `[L, R]` in increasing order.

The upper bound `R` can be as large as about `10¹²`, but the window width `R − L` is small (say up to `10⁶`). A standard sieve sized to `R` would not fit in memory, so you must sieve the window directly using only the primes up to `√R`.
questions.title: Segmented Sieve
constraints: 1 ≤ L ≤ R ≤ 10¹² (R is huge; R − L is the part that fits in memory)
0 ≤ R − L ≤ 10⁶ (window width — the boolean buffer is O(R − L))
L may equal 1 → 1 is not prime and must be excluded

questions.question:
Given an `m x n` integer matrix, if an element is `0`, set its **entire row and column** to `0`'s.

You must do it ***in place***.

A naive O(mn) extra-space solution exists; a follow-up asks for an O(m + n) solution, and a true ***constant-space*** solution is the goal.
questions.title: Set Matrix Zeroes
constraints: Mutation must be in place; the O(1)-space solution is the target

questions.question:
Given an integer `n`, return all prime numbers in the range `[2, n]` in increasing order.

A **prime** is an integer greater than 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself.

A closely related framing asks only for the **count** of primes strictly less than `n` (LeetCode 204, *Count Primes*) — the algorithm is identical; you just tally the survivors instead of collecting them.
questions.title: Sieve of Eratosthenes
constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 5 × 10⁶ (typical interview bound; sieve memory is O(n))
n may be 0 or 1 → return an empty list (no primes)

questions.question:
Given an `m x n` `matrix`, return ***all elements of the matrix in spiral order***.

Spiral order means: start at the top-left, walk **right** across the top row, **down** the right column, **left** across the bottom row, **up** the left column, then repeat one ring deeper until every cell is visited.
questions.title: Spiral Matrix
constraints: The matrix may be rectangular (m ≠ n is allowed)

questions.question:
Given a non-negative integer `x`, return the **square root of `x` rounded down to the nearest integer**. The returned integer should be non-negative as well.

You **must not use any built-in exponent function or operator** (such as `pow(x, 0.5)` or `x ** 0.5`).
questions.title: Sqrt(x)
constraints: x fits in a 32-bit signed integer

questions.question:
Given a non-negative integer `n`, return the sum of its digits.

Clarify whether the interviewer wants a **single** pass (e.g. `38 → 3 + 8 = 11`) or the **repeated** digit sum until one digit remains — the *digital root* (e.g. `38 → 11 → 2`).
questions.title: Sum of Digits (Digital Root)
constraints: n fits in a 64-bit integer; for larger inputs treat n as a string
If negatives are permitted, operate on |n|

questions.question:
You are given `p` queries; each query is an integer `n`. For each, determine whether `n` is a prime number and print **"Prime"** or **"Not prime"** accordingly.

The task is explicitly about **time complexity**: a naive O(n) check is too slow for large `n`, so you must test primality in **O(√n)** per query.
questions.title: Time Complexity: Primality
constraints: Each query must run in O(√n)
1 is not prime; 2 is the smallest prime
Output is exactly "Prime" or "Not prime" per query

questions.question:
A bracket is any one of `(`, `)`, `{`, `}`, `[`, or `]`. Two brackets are a **matched pair** when an opening bracket occurs to the left of a closing bracket of the **exact same type**.

Given a string `s` containing only these six characters, determine whether the sequence is **balanced**: every opening bracket has a corresponding closing bracket of the same type, and pairs are properly nested (the most recently opened bracket is the first one closed).

Return `true` if balanced, `false` otherwise.
questions.title: Balanced Brackets
constraints: s consists only of the characters ()[]{}
An empty inner sequence is fine — '()' is balanced
Return a boolean (some variants ask for the string 'YES'/'NO')

questions.question:
Given a string `s` representing a valid expression, implement a basic calculator to evaluate it, and return *the result of the evaluation*.

The expression string contains non-negative integers, `'+'`, `'-'`, `'('`, `')'`, and empty spaces `' '`. The integer division should truncate toward zero (not relevant here — there is no division).

**Note:** You are **not** allowed to use any built-in function which evaluates strings as mathematical expressions, such as `eval()`.
questions.title: Basic Calculator
constraints: '+' is not used as a unary operation (i.e. "+1" and "+(2 + 3)" are invalid)
'-' could be used as a unary operation (i.e. "-1" and "-(2 + 3)" are valid)
There will be no two consecutive operators in the input
Every number and running calculation will fit in a signed 32-bit integer

questions.question: Given an array of integers `temperatures` represents the daily temperatures, return an array `answer` such that `answer[i]` is the number of days you have to wait after the `i`-th day to get a warmer temperature. If there is no future day for which this is possible, keep `answer[i] == 0` instead.
questions.title: Daily Temperatures

questions.question:
You are given three stacks of cylinders, each cylinder having a positive integer height. The stacks are described top-to-bottom (the first number in each array is the cylinder currently on **top**).

In one operation you may remove the cylinder on the top of any stack. Find the **maximum possible height** such that all three stacks have exactly that total height after some removals. A height of `0` (all stacks emptied) is always achievable, so an answer always exists.

Return that maximum equal height.
questions.title: Equal Stacks
constraints: 0 ≤ n1, n2, n3 ≤ 10⁵ (number of cylinders in each stack)
Input lists are given top-to-bottom: index 0 is the top cylinder

questions.question:
You are given an array of strings `tokens` that represents an arithmetic expression in a **Reverse Polish Notation**.

Evaluate the expression. Return an integer that represents the value of the expression.

Note that:

- The valid operators are `'+'`, `'-'`, `'*'`, and `'/'`.
- Each operand may be an integer or another expression.
- The division between two integers always **truncates toward zero**.
- There will not be any division by zero.
- The input represents a valid arithmetic expression in RPN.
- The answer and all intermediate calculations fit in a 32-bit integer.
questions.title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
constraints: tokens[i] is either an operator '+', '-', '*', '/', or an integer in the range [-200, 200]
The input is a valid RPN expression
Division truncates toward zero; no division by zero occurs

questions.question: Given `n` pairs of parentheses, write a function to generate all combinations of **well-formed parentheses**.
questions.title: Generate Parentheses

questions.question:
You are given an array `heights` representing the heights of bars in a histogram, where each bar has width `1`. Find the area of the **largest rectangle** that can be formed within the bounds of the histogram.

The rectangle must be axis-aligned and made of consecutive bars; its height is limited by the **shortest** bar it spans.
questions.title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
constraints: Area can exceed 32-bit range → use 64-bit (long) for the running maximum

questions.question:
You have an empty stack. Process `q` queries, each of one of three types:

- `1 x` — push the integer `x` onto the stack.
- `2` — pop the element on top of the stack.
- `3` — print the **maximum** element currently in the stack.

All type-3 queries must run in O(1). Print the answer to each type-3 query on its own line.
questions.title: Maximum Element
constraints: Type 2 (pop) is only issued when the stack is non-empty
Type 3 (max) is only issued when the stack is non-empty

questions.question:
You are given an array `arr` of `n` integers. For a window (contiguous subarray) you take its minimum. For every window **size** from 1 to n, consider all windows of that size and take the **maximum** of their minimums.

Return an array of `n` values where the value at index `w − 1` is the maximum-of-minimums over all windows of size `w`.
questions.title: Min Max Riddle
constraints: Output has exactly n values (one per window size 1..n)
An O(n²) solution times out — O(n) or O(n log n) is required

questions.question:
Design a stack that supports push, pop, top, and retrieving the minimum element in constant time.

Implement the `MinStack` class:

- `MinStack()` initializes the stack object.
- `void push(int val)` pushes the element `val` onto the stack.
- `void pop()` removes the element on the top of the stack.
- `int top()` gets the top element of the stack.
- `int getMin()` retrieves the minimum element in the stack.

You must implement a solution with `O(1)` time complexity for each function.
questions.title: Min Stack

examples.input: push(-2), push(0), push(-3), getMin(), pop(), top(), getMin()

constraints: pop, top and getMin are always called on non-empty stacks
At most 3 * 10⁴ calls will be made to push, pop, top, and getMin

questions.question:
There are `n` plants in a row, each treated with some amount of pesticide. After each day, any plant with **more** pesticide than the plant immediately to its **left** dies (these deaths all happen at the end of the day, simultaneously). When plants die, the remaining plants shift together so each plant's left neighbour may change for the next day.

Given the initial pesticide levels `p`, determine the **number of days** after which no plant dies (i.e., the number of days on which at least one plant dies).
questions.title: Poisonous Plants
constraints: A plant dies only if its pesticide is STRICTLY greater than its current left neighbour's
Deaths within a day are simultaneous; survivors compact before the next day
Return the number of days until a day occurs with zero deaths (0 if no plant ever dies)

questions.question:
Implement a first-in-first-out (FIFO) **queue** using only two **stacks**. The implemented queue must support all the standard operations:

- `enqueue(x)` — add element `x` to the back of the queue.
- `dequeue()` — remove and return the element at the front of the queue.
- `peek()` — return the element at the front without removing it.
- `empty()` — return whether the queue is empty.

You may only use the standard stack operations: push to top, pop from top, peek at top, size, and is-empty.
questions.title: Queue Using Two Stacks
constraints: At most 10⁵ calls total across enqueue, dequeue, peek, empty
dequeue and peek are only called on a non-empty queue
Only stack operations may be used internally — no native queue/deque

questions.question:
Implement a simple text editor over an initially empty string `S`. Process `q` operations of four types:

- `1 W` — append the string `W` to the end of `S`.
- `2 k` — delete the last `k` characters of `S`.
- `3 k` — print the `k`-th character of `S` (1-indexed).
- `4` — undo the last *not-yet-undone* append or delete, reverting `S` to its previous value.

Print the result of each type-3 operation on its own line.
questions.title: Simple Text Editor
constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ |S| for delete and print operations
Total length of all appended strings ≤ 10⁶
Every type-4 (undo) has a matching prior append or delete to revert
Operations should be efficient (amortised near O(1) per op, O(length) per append)

questions.question:
You are given an **absolute** path for a Unix-style file system, which always begins with a slash `'/'`. Transform this absolute path into its **simplified canonical path**.

In a Unix-style file system, a period `'.'` refers to the current directory, a double period `'..'` refers to the directory up a level, and any multiple consecutive slashes (i.e. `'//'` or `'///'`) are treated as a single slash `'/'`. For this problem, any other format of periods such as `'...'` or `'....'` are treated as valid directory or file names.

The simplified canonical path should follow these rules:

- The path must start with a single slash `'/'`.
- Directories within the path must be separated by exactly one slash `'/'`.
- The path must not end with a slash `'/'`, unless it is the root directory.
- The path must not have any single or double periods (`'.'` and `'..'`) used to denote the current or parent directory.

Return the **simplified canonical path**.
questions.title: Simplify Path
constraints: path consists of English letters, digits, period '.', slash '/' or '_'
path is a valid absolute Unix path (begins with '/')

questions.question:
A truck must complete a circular tour of `n` petrol pumps. Pump `i` gives `petrol[i]` units of fuel, and the distance from pump `i` to the next pump (pump `(i+1) mod n`) costs `distance[i]` units of fuel (1 unit per km). The truck has an unlimited tank and starts empty.

Find the **index of the first petrol pump** from which the truck can start and complete the full circular tour, returning to the start. It is guaranteed that a unique solution exists.
questions.title: Truck Tour
constraints: A valid starting pump is guaranteed to exist (total petrol ≥ total distance)
An O(n²) simulation times out — aim for O(n)
