questions.question:
Given a string `s` containing just the characters `'('`, `')'`, `'{'`, `'}'`, `'['` and `']'`, determine if the input string is **valid**.

An input string is valid if:

1. Open brackets must be closed by the same type of brackets.
2. Open brackets must be closed in the correct order.
3. Every close bracket has a corresponding open bracket of the same type.
questions.title: Valid Parentheses

questions.question:
You are given `number`, a list of `n` integers representing a stack of plates (front of the list is processed first each round), and an integer `q`.

Process `q` rounds. In round `i` (1-indexed) use the `i`-th prime `p_i` (so `p_1 = 2`, `p_2 = 3`, …). Scan the current pile: plates divisible by `p_i` go to pile `B_i`, the rest to pile `A_i`. After the round, the plates in `B_i` are placed on the answer pile (removed top-first / popped). The next round operates on `A_i`. After all `q` rounds, the plates left in `A_q` are placed on the answer pile (popped).

Return the answer pile from bottom to top (the order in which plates were placed).
questions.title: Waiter
constraints: Generate exactly the first q prime numbers

questions.question:
You are given a string `s` containing only the characters `A` and `B`. A string is **alternating** if no two adjacent characters are the same (e.g. `ABAB`, `BABA`).

In one operation you may delete any single character. Return the **minimum number of deletions** required to turn `s` into an alternating string.
questions.title: Alternating Characters
constraints: s consists only of the characters 'A' and 'B'
Only deletions are allowed (no insertions or replacements)

questions.question:
Given a string `s`, split it into two halves: the first half `a` and the second half `b`. Determine the **minimum number of character changes** needed to make `b` an anagram of `a` (changing a character means replacing it with any other character).

If the length of `s` is **odd**, the two halves cannot have equal length, so it is impossible — return `-1`.
questions.title: Anagram
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters only
A 'change' replaces one character with any other (no insert/delete)

questions.question: Given an unencrypted string `s` and a non-negative integer `k`, encrypt the string with a Caesar cipher: **shift each letter forward by `k` positions** in the alphabet, wrapping around from `z` back to `a` (and `Z` to `A`). Case must be preserved, and **non-letter characters are left unchanged**. Return the encrypted string.
questions.title: Caesar Cipher
constraints: 0 ≤ k ≤ 10⁹  (k can be far larger than 26)
s may contain letters, digits, spaces, and punctuation
Letter case must be preserved in the output

questions.question:
A word in CamelCase notation starts with a lowercase letter; the start of each subsequent word is marked by an uppercase letter. For example, `oneTwoThree` has three words.

Given a camelCase string `s`, return the **number of words** it contains.
questions.title: CamelCase
constraints: s contains only English letters (a–z, A–Z)
The first character is lowercase (standard camelCase, not PascalCase)

questions.question:
Consider a number as a sequence of its decimal digits. A number is **colorful** if the product of the digits of **every contiguous subsequence (substring)** of its digit-sequence is **distinct**.

For example, `3245` has digit-runs `3, 2, 4, 5, 32, 24, 45, 324, 245, 3245` with products `3, 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 20, 24, 40, 120` — all different — so it is colorful.

Given a non-negative integer `n`, return `"YES"` if it is colorful, otherwise `"NO"`.
questions.title: Colorful Number
constraints: Treat n as the string of its decimal digits
Products are of contiguous digit runs only

questions.question:
Given a string `s` of length `n`, return the number of **distinct non-empty substrings** of `s`.

A substring is a contiguous slice `s[i..j]`. Two substrings are the same if they are equal as strings, regardless of where they occur. Count each distinct value once.
questions.title: Count Distinct Substrings
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵ (the optimal); the hashing baseline only survives n ≤ ~3000
Answer can be up to n(n+1)/2 ≈ 5×10⁹ for n = 10⁵ — use 64-bit
Substrings are contiguous; subsequences are a different problem

questions.question:
An avid hiker keeps detailed records of their hikes. During the last hike that took exactly `steps` steps, for every step it was noted if it was an **uphill** `'U'` or a **downhill** `'D'` step. Hikes always start and end at sea level, and each step up or down represents a `1` unit change in altitude.

We define the following terms:

- A **mountain** is a sequence of consecutive steps **above** sea level, starting with a step up from sea level and ending with a step down to sea level.
- A **valley** is a sequence of consecutive steps **below** sea level, starting with a step down from sea level and ending with a step up to sea level.

Given the sequence of up and down steps during a hike, find and return **the number of valleys** walked through.
questions.title: Counting Valleys
constraints: The number of 'U' steps equals the number of 'D' steps (the hike starts and ends at sea level)

questions.question:
Design an algorithm to encode **a list of strings** to **a single string**. The encoded string is then sent over the network and is decoded back to the original list of strings.

Implement the `encode` and `decode` methods:

- `string encode(List<string> strs)` encodes a list of strings to a single string.
- `List<string> decode(string s)` decodes a single string back to the original list of strings.

You are not allowed to solve the problem using any serialization library functions (such as `eval`).
questions.title: Encode and Decode Strings
constraints: strs[i] contains any possible characters out of 256 valid ASCII characters
encode(decode(s)) must return the original list exactly (round-trip lossless)

questions.question: Given two strings `needle` and `haystack`, return the index of the **first occurrence** of `needle` in `haystack`, or `-1` if `needle` is not part of `haystack`.
questions.title: Find the Index of the First Occurrence in a String
constraints: haystack and needle consist of only lowercase English characters

questions.question: Given a string `s`, find the **first non-repeating character** in it and return its index. If it does not exist, return `-1`.
questions.title: First Unique Character in a String
constraints: s consists of only lowercase English letters

questions.question:
A string is **funny** if, comparing it with its reverse, the absolute difference between the ASCII values of every pair of adjacent characters is preserved.

Formally, let `r = reverse(s)`. For every position `i` from `1` to `|s| − 1`, the string is funny if `|s[i] − s[i−1]| == |r[i] − r[i−1]|`, where `s[i]` denotes the ASCII value of the character.

Return `"Funny"` if the condition holds for all `i`, and `"Not Funny"` otherwise.
questions.title: Funny String
constraints: s consists of lowercase (or mixed) English letters
Differences are taken over ASCII / code-point values

questions.question:
You are given an array of `n` rocks, each represented by a non-empty string of lowercase letters. Each letter inside a rock is a **mineral**.

A mineral is called a **gem element** (or gemstone) if it occurs **at least once in every rock**.

Return the number of distinct gem elements — that is, how many letters appear in all `n` rocks.
questions.title: Gemstones
constraints: Each rock string consists of lowercase English letters a–z

questions.question:
Given an array of strings `strs`, group the anagrams together. You can return the answer in **any order**.

An **anagram** is a word formed by rearranging the letters of another, using all the original letters exactly once.
questions.title: Group Anagrams
constraints: strs[i] consists of lowercase English letters

questions.question:
Given a string `s`, determine whether it contains the word `"hackerrank"` as a **subsequence** — that is, whether you can obtain `"hackerrank"` by deleting zero or more characters from `s` without reordering the rest.

Return `"YES"` if it does, `"NO"` otherwise.
questions.title: HackerRank in a String
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
The target word is the fixed string "hackerrank" (length 10)

questions.question:
Roman numerals are represented by seven symbols: `I`, `V`, `X`, `L`, `C`, `D` and `M`, with values `1, 5, 10, 50, 100, 500, 1000`.

Roman numerals are usually written largest to smallest from left to right. However, the numeral for four is not `IIII` but `IV` — the smaller `I` placed before the larger `V` and subtracted. The same subtractive principle applies in six cases: `IV` (4), `IX` (9), `XL` (40), `XC` (90), `CD` (400), and `CM` (900).

Given an integer, convert it to a Roman numeral.
questions.title: Integer to Roman

questions.question:
Given two strings `s` and `t`, return `true` if `s` is a **subsequence** of `t`, or `false` otherwise.

A **subsequence** of a string is a new string that is formed from the original string by deleting some (can be none) of the characters without disturbing the relative positions of the remaining characters. (i.e., `"ace"` is a subsequence of `"abcde"` while `"aec"` is not.)

**Follow up:** Suppose there are lots of incoming `s`, say `s1, s2, ..., sk` where `k >= 10⁹`, and you want to check one by one to see if `t` has its subsequence. In this scenario, how would you change your code?
questions.title: Is Subsequence
constraints: s and t consist only of lowercase English letters

questions.question:
Given two strings `s` and `t`, determine if they are **isomorphic**.

Two strings `s` and `t` are isomorphic if the characters in `s` can be replaced to get `t`.

All occurrences of a character must be replaced with another character while preserving the order of characters. ***No two characters may map to the same character***, but a character may map to itself.
questions.title: Isomorphic Strings
constraints: s and t consist of any valid ASCII character

questions.question:
Given a string `s` consisting of words and spaces, return the **length of the last word** in the string.

A **word** is a maximal substring consisting of non-space characters only.
questions.title: Length of Last Word

examples.input: s = "   fly me   to   the moon  "

constraints: s consists of only English letters and spaces ' '
There is at least one word in s

questions.question:
Given a string `s`, return its **1-based rank** among all distinct permutations of its characters, listed in lexicographic (dictionary) order.

The smallest permutation has rank 1. If `s` contains repeated characters, count each distinct arrangement once.
questions.title: Lexicographic Rank of a String
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 20 if using 64-bit factorials; larger n needs big integers or modular arithmetic

questions.question:
Write a function to find the longest common prefix string amongst an array of strings `strs`.

If there is no common prefix, return an empty string `""`.

A *prefix* must be anchored at the start of every string — `"fl"` is a prefix of `"flower"`, but `"low"` is not.
questions.title: Longest Common Prefix
constraints: strs[i] consists of only lowercase English letters
An individual string may be empty (length 0)

questions.question:
Given a string `s`, return the **longest substring** of `s` that is a palindrome (reads identically forwards and backwards).

If several palindromes share the maximum length, returning any one of them is acceptable. A single character is a palindrome of length 1.
questions.title: Longest Palindromic Substring — Manacher's Algorithm
constraints: ASCII characters; the separator `#` must not appear in s (or use a sentinel not in the alphabet)
Return any one longest palindrome if there are ties

questions.question:
You are given a string `s` and an integer `k`. You can choose any character of the string and change it to any other uppercase English character. You can perform this operation at most `k` times.

Return the length of the **longest substring** containing the **same letter** you can get after performing the above operations.
questions.title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
constraints: s consists of only uppercase English letters

questions.question:
Given a string `s`, find the length of the **longest substring** without repeating characters.

A substring is a contiguous, non-empty sequence of characters within the string.
questions.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
constraints: s consists of English letters, digits, symbols and spaces

questions.question:
Given two strings `a` and `b`, find the **minimum number of character deletions** required to make `a` and `b` anagrams of each other. You may delete characters from **either** string.

Two strings are anagrams if they contain the same characters with the same multiplicities (in any order).
questions.title: Making Anagrams
constraints: a and b consist of lowercase English letters only
Deletions are allowed from both strings

questions.question:
A probe on Mars sends the message `"SOS"` repeated, but cosmic interference may have altered some letters during transmission. You receive a string `s` whose length is a multiple of 3, formed from the original `"SOS"` repeated `|s| / 3` times.

Return the **number of letters that were altered** — i.e. the number of positions in `s` that differ from the expected repeated `"SOS"` pattern.
questions.title: Mars Exploration
constraints: s consists of uppercase English letters only
The original message is "SOS" repeated |s| / 3 times

questions.question:
Given two strings `s` and `t` of lengths `m` and `n`, return the **minimum window substring** of `s` such that every character in `t` (**including duplicates**) is included in the window. If there is no such substring, return the empty string `""`.

The test cases are generated such that the answer is **unique**.
questions.title: Minimum Window Substring
constraints: s and t consist of uppercase and lowercase English letters

questions.question:
Given a string `s`, determine the **index** of a character that can be removed to make `s` a palindrome. There is **always a valid solution**: either the string is already a palindrome, or removing exactly one character makes it one.

If `s` is already a palindrome, return `-1`. Otherwise return the 0-based index of the character to remove. If multiple indices work, any valid one is acceptable.
questions.title: Palindrome Index
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
A valid answer always exists (remove at most one character)
Return any valid index, or −1 if already a palindrome

questions.question:
A **pangram** is a sentence that contains every letter of the English alphabet at least once, regardless of case.

Given a string `s`, determine whether it is a pangram. Return `"pangram"` if it uses all 26 letters a–z, and `"not pangram"` otherwise.

The sentence may contain spaces and is case-insensitive (`A` and `a` count as the same letter).
questions.title: Pangrams

examples.input: s = "We promptly judged antique ivory buckles for the next prize"
s = "We promptly judged antique ivory buckles for the prize"

constraints: s consists of English letters (upper or lower case) and spaces

questions.question:
Given a text string `t` of length `n` and a pattern string `p` of length `m`, return **all starting indices** `i` (0-based) such that `t[i..i+m-1] == p`.

Occurrences may overlap (e.g. pattern `aa` in text `aaaa` occurs at indices 0, 1, 2). If the pattern never appears, return an empty list.
questions.title: Pattern Search — KMP (Knuth–Morris–Pratt)
constraints: Strings consist of printable ASCII characters
Overlapping occurrences must all be reported
An empty pattern is out of scope — assume m ≥ 1

questions.question:
Given a text `t` of length `n` and a pattern `p` of length `m`, return **all starting indices** in `t` where `p` occurs.

Solve it with the Z-function: construct `s = p + '#' + t`, compute the Z-array of `s`, and report every index `i` with `z[i] == m`, mapped back to text coordinates. Overlapping occurrences must all be reported.
questions.title: Pattern Search — Z-Algorithm
constraints: There exists at least one character (the separator `#`) that appears in neither `p` nor `t`
Strings are printable ASCII unless stated otherwise

questions.question:
Given two strings `s1` and `s2`, return `true` if `s2` contains a **permutation** of `s1`, or `false` otherwise.

In other words, return `true` if one of `s1`'s permutations is a **substring** of `s2`.
questions.title: Permutation in String
constraints: s1 and s2 consist of lowercase English letters

questions.question:
Given a text `t` of length `n` and a pattern `p` of length `m`, return **all starting indices** in `t` where `p` occurs, using a rolling hash.

Report overlapping occurrences. Your hash equality must be confirmed by an actual character comparison so that a hash collision never produces a wrong answer.
questions.title: Rabin–Karp Substring Search (Rolling Hash)
constraints: Strings are ASCII; treat each character's code as its numeric value
Use a large prime modulus to keep collision probability low

questions.question:
Given two strings `ransomNote` and `magazine`, return `true` if `ransomNote` can be constructed by using the letters from `magazine`, and `false` otherwise.

**Each letter in `magazine` can only be used once** in `ransomNote`.
questions.title: Ransom Note
constraints: ransomNote and magazine consist of lowercase English letters only

questions.question:
There is a string `s` of lowercase English letters that is repeated infinitely many times. Given an integer `n`, find and print **the number of letter 'a'** in the first `n` characters of the infinitely repeating string.

For example, if `s = "abcac"` and `n = 10`, the first 10 characters are `"abcacabcac"`, which contains 4 occurrences of 'a'.
questions.title: Repeated String
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10¹²  (n can be far larger than |s|)
s consists of lowercase English letters only

questions.question:
A string `A` was produced from a secret string `s` by the procedure `A = merge(reverse(s), shuffle(s))`, where:

- `reverse(s)` reverses `s`,
- `shuffle(s)` is some permutation of `s`,
- `merge(p, q)` interleaves `p` and `q` preserving the internal order of each.

Given `A`, recover the **lexicographically smallest** possible `s`.
questions.title: Reverse Shuffle Merge
constraints: A consists of lowercase English letters only
Every character occurs an even number of times in A
Return the lexicographically smallest valid s

questions.question:
Given an input string `s`, reverse the order of the **words**.

A *word* is a maximal sequence of non-space characters. The words in `s` are separated by at least one space.

Return a string of the words in reverse order concatenated by a **single** space.

Note: `s` may contain leading or trailing spaces or multiple spaces between two words. The returned string should have a single space separating the words and **no** leading or trailing spaces.
questions.title: Reverse Words in a String
constraints: s contains English letters (upper and lower case), digits, and spaces ' '
There is at least one word in s
Follow-up: can you solve it in O(1) extra space if s is a mutable character array?

questions.question:
Roman numerals are represented by seven symbols: `I`, `V`, `X`, `L`, `C`, `D`, `M` with values 1, 5, 10, 50, 100, 500, 1000.

Usually a numeral is written largest-to-smallest left to right and you add the values. But six cases use *subtraction*: `IV` = 4, `IX` = 9, `XL` = 40, `XC` = 90, `CD` = 400, `CM` = 900 — a smaller symbol placed before a larger one is subtracted.

Given a Roman numeral string `s`, convert it to an integer.
questions.title: Roman to Integer
constraints: s contains only the characters I, V, X, L, C, D, M
s is guaranteed to be a valid Roman numeral in the range [1, 3999]

questions.question:
A string of digits is **beautiful** if it can be split into a sequence of **two or more** positive integers satisfying:

1. Each number (after the first) is exactly **one greater** than the previous number.
2. No number contains a **leading zero**.

Given a string `s`, determine whether it is beautiful. If it is, output `"YES"` followed by the **first** number of the sequence; otherwise output `"NO"`.
questions.title: Separate the Numbers
constraints: Numbers may be large enough to require 64-bit (long) arithmetic
No leading zeros are allowed in any number of the sequence

questions.question:
Two strings are **anagrams** of each other if the letters of one can be rearranged to form the other.

Given a string `s`, count the number of **pairs of substrings** of `s` that are anagrams of each other. A substring is identified by its start and end positions, so two substrings with identical content but different positions are distinct.

Return the total number of unordered anagrammatic substring pairs.
questions.title: Sherlock and Anagrams
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
Substrings are compared by content; position distinguishes otherwise-equal substrings
Pairs are unordered: (A, B) and (B, A) count once

questions.question:
Watson asks Sherlock whether a string `s` is **valid**. A string is valid when **all characters appear the same number of times**. It is *also* valid when removing **just one character at one index** leaves every remaining character appearing the same number of times.

Return `"YES"` if `s` is valid and `"NO"` otherwise.
questions.title: Sherlock and the Valid String
constraints: s contains lowercase English letters only
At most one character may be removed (zero or one)

questions.question:
A string is **valid** if all of its characters appear the **same number of times**. It is also valid if you can remove **exactly one character** at **one index** in the string, and the remaining characters then all appear the same number of times.

Given a string `s`, return `"YES"` if it is valid, otherwise `"NO"`.
questions.title: Sherlock and the Valid String
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters only
You may delete at most one character total (zero or one)

questions.question: There is a collection of input strings and a collection of query strings. For each query string, determine **how many times** it occurs in the list of input strings. Return the counts in the **same order** as the queries.
questions.title: Sparse Arrays
constraints: All strings consist of lowercase English letters

questions.question:
A string is a **special palindrome** if either:

1. **All** of its characters are the same (e.g. `"aaa"`), or
2. All characters **except the middle one** are the same, and the middle character differs (e.g. `"aadaa"`).

Given a string `s` of length `n`, count how many **substrings** of `s` are special palindromes (substrings at different positions count separately even if equal).
questions.title: Special String Again
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
Count substrings by position — identical content at different indices counts multiple times
The answer can be large; use a 64-bit integer

questions.question:
Implement the `myAtoi(string s)` function, which converts a string to a 32-bit signed integer.

The algorithm is:

1. **Whitespace**: ignore leading whitespace (`' '`).
2. **Signedness**: read the next character if it is `'-'` or `'+'`, determining the sign. If neither, the result is positive.
3. **Conversion**: read digits until a non-digit character (or end of input) is reached. The rest of the string is ignored.
4. **Rounding**: if the integer is out of the 32-bit signed range `[-2³¹, 2³¹ − 1]`, clamp it so values below `-2³¹` become `-2147483648` and values above `2³¹ − 1` become `2147483647`.

Return the resulting integer.
questions.title: String to Integer (atoi)
constraints: s consists of English letters (upper/lower), digits 0–9, ' ', '+', '-', and '.'
Only the leading numeric portion is parsed; trailing characters are ignored

questions.question:
A password is **strong** if it satisfies all of the following:

- has at least **6** characters,
- contains at least **one digit** (`0–9`),
- contains at least **one lowercase** letter,
- contains at least **one uppercase** letter,
- contains at least **one special** character from `!@#$%^&*()-+`.

Given the current password string `s`, return the **minimum number of characters** you must add to make it strong.
questions.title: Strong Password
constraints: s consists of characters from a–z, A–Z, 0–9, and the special set !@#$%^&*()-+
You may only add characters (not remove or replace)

questions.question:
You are given a string `s` and an array of strings `words`. All the strings of `words` are of the ***same length***.

A **concatenated substring** in `s` is a substring that contains all the strings of any permutation of `words` concatenated.

For example, if `words = ["ab", "cd", "ef"]`, then `"abcdef"`, `"abefcd"`, `"cdabef"`, `"cdefab"`, `"efabcd"`, and `"efcdab"` are all concatenated strings. `"acdbef"` is not because it is not the concatenation of any permutation.

Return the **starting indices** of all the concatenated substrings in `s`. You can return the answer in any order.
questions.title: Substring with Concatenation of All Words
constraints: All words[i] are of the same length
s and words[i] consist of lowercase English letters

questions.question:
Given an array of strings `words` and a width `maxWidth`, format the text such that each line has exactly `maxWidth` characters and is fully (left and right) justified.

You should pack your words in a greedy approach; that is, pack as many words as you can in each line. Pad extra spaces `' '` when necessary so that each line has exactly `maxWidth` characters.

Extra spaces between words should be distributed as evenly as possible. If the number of spaces on a line does not divide evenly between words, the empty slots on the **left** will be assigned more spaces than the slots on the right.

For the **last line** of text, it should be **left-justified**, and no extra space is inserted between words. Similarly, a line with **only one word** is left-justified.
questions.title: Text Justification
constraints: words[i] consists of only English letters and symbols

questions.question:
You are given a string `s`. You may delete **all** occurrences of one or more characters (i.e. remove entire letters). After deletions, the resulting string `t` is **valid** if:

1. `t` contains **exactly two distinct characters**, and
2. no two adjacent characters of `t` are the same (it alternates, e.g. `"ababab"`).

Return the length of the **longest** valid string obtainable, or `0` if no such string exists.
questions.title: Two Characters
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
You may delete every occurrence of any chosen letters
The kept string must alternate between exactly two distinct letters

questions.question:
Given two strings, determine whether they share a **common substring**. A substring may be as small as a single character.

For each pair return the string `"YES"` if the two strings share any common substring, and `"NO"` if they do not.
questions.title: Two Strings
constraints: Both strings consist of lowercase English letters only

questions.question:
Given two strings `s` and `t`, return `true` if `t` is an anagram of `s`, and `false` otherwise.

An **anagram** is a word formed by rearranging the letters of another, using all the original letters exactly once.
questions.title: Valid Anagram
constraints: s and t consist of lowercase English letters
Follow-up: what if the inputs contain Unicode characters?

questions.question:
Given a string `s`, return `true` if `s` can be a palindrome after deleting **at most one** character from it.

A palindrome reads the same forward and backward. Deleting at most one character means you may delete zero or one character.
questions.title: Valid Palindrome II
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters only

questions.question:
A phrase is a **palindrome** if, after converting all uppercase letters into lowercase letters and removing all non-alphanumeric characters, it reads the same forward and backward.

Given a string `s`, return `true` if it is a palindrome, or `false` otherwise. Alphanumeric characters include letters and numbers.
questions.title: Valid Palindrome

examples.input: s = "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"

constraints: s consists only of printable ASCII characters

questions.question:
The **weight** of a character is its 1-based position in the alphabet: `a = 1, b = 2, …, z = 26`. A **uniform** string is one made of a single repeated character (e.g. `"ccc"`). The **weight of a uniform string** is the character weight times its length (e.g. `"ccc" = 3 × 3 = 9`).

Given a string `s` and a list of integer `queries`, for each query determine whether there exists a **uniform substring** of `s` whose weight equals the query. Output `"Yes"` or `"No"` for each query.
questions.title: Weighted Uniform Strings
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters

questions.question:
Given a `pattern` and a string `s`, find if `s` follows the same pattern.

Here **follow** means a full match, such that there is a ***bijection*** between a letter in `pattern` and a non-empty word in `s`.

Specifically:

- Each letter in `pattern` maps to exactly one unique word in `s`.
- Each unique word in `s` maps to exactly one letter in `pattern`.
- No two letters map to the same word, and no two words map to the same letter.
questions.title: Word Pattern
constraints: pattern contains only lowercase English letters
s contains only lowercase English letters and single spaces between words
s does not contain leading or trailing spaces
Each word in s is separated by exactly one space

questions.question:
The string `"PAYPALISHIRING"` is written in a zigzag pattern on a given number of rows like this (you may want to display this pattern in a fixed font for better legibility):

```
P   A   H   N
A P L S I I G
Y   I   R
```

And then read line by line: `"PAHNAPLSIIGYIR"`.

Write the code that will take a string and make this conversion given a number of rows.
questions.title: Zigzag Conversion
constraints: s consists of English letters (lower-case and upper-case), ',' and '.'

questions.question:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, return the **average value of the nodes on each level** in the form of an array.

Answers within `10⁻⁵` of the actual answer will be accepted.
questions.title: Average of Levels in Binary Tree
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 10⁴]
The answer is an array of doubles, one per level, top to bottom

questions.question:
Given a binary tree, determine if it is **height-balanced**.

A height-balanced binary tree is defined as a binary tree in which the left and right subtrees of *every* node differ in height by no more than 1.
questions.title: Balanced Binary Tree
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 5000]
An empty tree is balanced (return true)

questions.question:
You are given a rooted tree with `n` nodes (the parent of each node, with the root having no parent). Answer up to `q` queries, each asking for the ***lowest common ancestor*** of two nodes `a` and `b` — the deepest node that is an ancestor of both.

Preprocess once, then answer every query in ***O(log n)***.
questions.title: Lowest Common Ancestor with Binary Lifting
constraints: The tree is rooted and static (does not change between queries)
Nodes are 0-indexed (or 1-indexed); the root has a sentinel parent

questions.question:
Given the `root` of a binary search tree and a value `v`, **insert** `v` into the BST and return the root of the updated tree.

A binary search tree keeps, for every node, all smaller values in its left subtree and all larger values in its right subtree. You may assume `v` is not already present.
questions.title: Binary Search Tree: Insertion
constraints: 0 ≤ number of nodes ≤ 500 (the tree may be empty)
The value to insert is not already in the tree
The BST ordering invariant holds before insertion

questions.question:
Given the `root` of a binary search tree and two node values `v1` and `v2`, return the **lowest common ancestor (LCA)** of the two nodes — the deepest node that has both `v1` and `v2` as descendants (a node is a descendant of itself).

You may assume both values exist in the tree.
questions.title: Binary Search Tree: Lowest Common Ancestor
constraints: All node values are unique (it is a valid BST)
Both v1 and v2 are guaranteed to be present in the tree

questions.question:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, return ***the level order traversal*** of its nodes' values. (i.e., from left to right, level by level).

The result is a list of lists: the i-th inner list contains all node values at depth i, ordered left to right.
questions.title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 2000]
The tree may be empty (root == null)

questions.question:
A ***path*** in a binary tree is a sequence of nodes where each pair of adjacent nodes in the sequence has an edge connecting them. A node can only appear in the sequence ***at most once***. Note that the path does not need to pass through the root.

The ***path sum*** of a path is the sum of the node's values in the path.

Given the `root` of a binary tree, return ***the maximum path sum of any non-empty path***.
questions.title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 3 × 10⁴]
The path is non-empty (at least one node) and node values may be negative

questions.question:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, imagine yourself standing on the ***right side*** of it. Return the values of the nodes you can see ordered from ***top to bottom***.

For each level of the tree, the visible node is the one furthest to the right at that depth.
questions.title: Binary Tree Right Side View
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 100]

questions.question:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, return the **inorder** traversal of its nodes' values.

Inorder means: recursively traverse the left subtree, visit the current node, then recursively traverse the right subtree. (Preorder and postorder are the natural variations the interviewer will ask you to produce next.)
questions.title: Binary Tree Traversal (In/Pre/Post)
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 100]
Stretch: solve it in O(1) extra space (Morris traversal)

questions.question: Given the `root` of a binary tree, return the **zigzag level order traversal** of its nodes' values. (i.e., from left to right, then right to left for the next level and alternate between).
questions.title: Binary Tree Zigzag Level Order Traversal
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 2000]
Output is a list of lists, one per level, with alternating within-row direction

questions.question:
Given a tree with `n` nodes, find a ***centroid***: a node such that, if it is removed, every connected component that remains has at most `⌊n/2⌋` nodes.

Return any centroid (there may be two adjacent ones). Your solution should run in ***O(n)***.
questions.title: Centroid of a Tree

examples.input: star: center 0 connected to 1,2,3,4 (n=5); find centroid

constraints: The graph is a tree: connected, n − 1 edges, no cycles
Nodes are 0-indexed; the tree is given as an edge list
A tree always has at least one centroid; even-n balanced trees have two adjacent centroids

questions.question:
Given two integer arrays `preorder` and `inorder` where `preorder` is the preorder traversal of a binary tree and `inorder` is the inorder traversal of the ***same tree***, construct and return the binary tree.

All values in the tree are unique.
questions.title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
constraints: preorder and inorder consist of unique values
inorder is a permutation of preorder; both describe the same valid binary tree

questions.question:
Given the `root` of a **complete** binary tree, return the number of nodes in the tree.

According to Wikipedia, every level of a complete binary tree, except possibly the last, is completely filled, and all nodes in the last level are as far **left** as possible. The last level can hold between `1` and `2^h` nodes inclusive (where `h` is the height of that last level).

Design an algorithm that runs in less than `O(n)` time complexity.
questions.title: Count Complete Tree Nodes
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 5 × 10⁴]
The tree is guaranteed to be complete

questions.question:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, return ***the length of the diameter*** of the tree.

The ***diameter*** of a binary tree is the length of the ***longest path*** between any two nodes in the tree. This path may or may not pass through the `root`.

The length of a path between two nodes is represented by the ***number of edges*** between them.
questions.title: Diameter of Binary Tree
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 10⁴]
The path length is counted in edges, so a single-node tree has diameter 0

questions.question:
You are given a rooted tree with `n` nodes, each holding a value. Support:

1. ***update(node, val)*** — change the value stored at `node`.
2. ***subtreeSum(node)*** — return the sum of values over `node` and all of its descendants.

Preprocess with an Euler tour so each subtree maps to a contiguous array range, then back the array with a Fenwick tree to make both operations ***O(log n)***.
questions.title: Euler Tour of a Tree (Subtree Flattening)
constraints: Up to 2 × 10⁵ interleaved update and subtreeSum calls
The tree is rooted and its shape is static
Sums fit in 64-bit (use long in Java)

questions.question:
Maintain a Fenwick tree (Binary Indexed Tree) over an array `a[1..n]` supporting:

1. ***update(i, delta)*** — add `delta` to `a[i]`.
2. ***prefix(i)*** — return `a[1] + a[2] + … + a[i]`.
3. ***rangeSum(l, r)*** — return `a[l] + … + a[r]`, computed as `prefix(r) − prefix(l − 1)`.

Each of the first two operations must run in ***O(log n)***. Explain the `lowbit = i & -i` trick that makes this work.
questions.title: Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree)
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵ (or larger; the structure scales to ~10⁶ comfortably)
Indices are 1-based: valid i is in [1, n]
Up to 10⁵ interleaved update and query calls
Sums fit in 64-bit (use long in Java)

questions.question:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, **flatten it into a 'linked list' in place**:

- The linked list should use the same `TreeNode` class where the `right` child pointer points to the next node and the `left` child pointer is always `null`.
- The linked list should be in the same order as a **preorder traversal** of the binary tree.
questions.title: Flatten Binary Tree to Linked List
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 2000]
Follow-up: can you flatten the tree in place using O(1) extra space?

questions.question:
You are given a rooted tree with `n` nodes, each holding a value. Support many queries of the form:

1. ***pathQuery(u, v)*** — aggregate (e.g. sum or max) of the values on the path from `u` to `v`.
2. ***update(node, val)*** — change the value at a node.

The tree's shape is fixed. Use heavy-light decomposition with a segment tree so each path query runs in ***O(log² n)*** and each update in ***O(log n)***.
questions.title: Heavy-Light Decomposition (Path Queries)

examples.input: path tree 0-1-2-3-4 (a chain), values=[1,2,3,4,5]; pathQuery(0,4) sum

constraints: Up to 10⁵ interleaved pathQuery and update calls
The tree is rooted and its shape does not change
Aggregate is associative (sum, max, min, gcd); values fit in 64-bit

questions.question:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, **invert** the tree, and return its root.

Inverting means producing the mirror image: for every node, its left and right subtrees are swapped.
questions.title: Invert Binary Tree
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 100]
An empty tree inverts to an empty tree

questions.question:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, determine whether it is a valid **binary search tree**.

For every node, all values in its left subtree must be strictly less than the node's value, and all values in its right subtree must be strictly greater. (HackerRank's version uses distinct values in the range 0 to 10000, so equality anywhere makes it invalid.)

Return `true` if the tree is a valid BST, otherwise `false`.
questions.title: Is This a Binary Search Tree?

examples.input: tree with root 3, left subtree {2,1}, right subtree {5,4,6}
root 3 with right child 5 whose LEFT child is 1

constraints: The BST property must hold strictly (no equal values allowed)

questions.question: Given the `root` of a binary search tree, and an integer `k`, return ***the k-th smallest value*** (1-indexed) of all the values of the nodes in the tree.
questions.title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
constraints: The number of nodes is n, with 1 ≤ k ≤ n ≤ 10⁴
The tree is a valid BST with unique values

questions.question:
Given a binary search tree (BST), find the lowest common ancestor (LCA) of two given nodes `p` and `q` in the BST.

The lowest common ancestor is defined between two nodes `p` and `q` as the lowest node in the tree that has both `p` and `q` as descendants (where we allow ***a node to be a descendant of itself***).

Both `p` and `q` exist in the BST and all node values are unique.
questions.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a BST
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [2, 10⁵]
p ≠ q, and both p and q exist in the BST

questions.question:
Given a binary tree, find the **lowest common ancestor (LCA)** of two given nodes `p` and `q` in the tree.

The lowest common ancestor is defined as the lowest node in the tree that has both `p` and `q` as descendants, where we allow **a node to be a descendant of itself** (so if `p` is an ancestor of `q`, the LCA of `p` and `q` is `p`).
questions.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [2, 10⁵]
p ≠ q and both p and q exist in the tree

questions.question:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, return its **maximum depth**.

A binary tree's maximum depth is the number of nodes along the longest path from the root node down to the farthest leaf node.
questions.title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 10⁴]

questions.question:
Given the `root` of a Binary Search Tree (BST), return the **minimum absolute difference between the values of any two different nodes** in the tree.

Note: This is the same as LeetCode 783, *Minimum Distance Between BST Nodes*.
questions.title: Minimum Absolute Difference in BST
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [2, 10⁴]
The tree is guaranteed to be a valid BST

questions.question:
Given the `root` of a binary tree and an integer `targetSum`, return `true` if the tree has a **root-to-leaf** path such that adding up all the values along the path equals `targetSum`.

A **leaf** is a node with no children.
questions.title: Path Sum
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 5000]

questions.question:
Given the roots of two binary trees `p` and `q`, write a function to check if they are **the same** or not.

Two binary trees are considered the same if they are structurally identical, and the nodes have the same value.
questions.title: Same Tree
constraints: The number of nodes in both trees is in the range [0, 100]
Two empty trees are considered the same

questions.question:
Design a data structure over an integer array `a[0..n-1]` that supports two operations efficiently after building:

1. ***rangeSum(l, r)*** — return the sum of `a[l] + a[l+1] + … + a[r]`.
2. ***update(i, val)*** — set `a[i] = val`.

The operations are interleaved and there can be up to 10⁵ of each. Build once, then answer every operation in ***O(log n)***.
questions.title: Segment Tree for Range Sum
constraints: Up to 10⁵ mixed update and rangeSum calls
0 ≤ l ≤ r ≤ n − 1 for every query
Values fit in 64-bit after summation (use long in Java)

questions.question:
Given the roots of two binary trees `root` and `subRoot`, return `true` if there is a subtree of `root` with the same structure and node values as `subRoot`, and `false` otherwise.

A subtree of a binary tree `tree` is a tree that consists of a node in `tree` and **all of this node's descendants**. The tree `tree` could also be considered as a subtree of itself.
questions.title: Subtree of Another Tree
constraints: The number of nodes in root is in the range [1, 2000]
The number of nodes in subRoot is in the range [1, 1000]
subRoot must match a node AND all of its descendants in root

questions.question:
You are given the `root` of a binary tree containing digits from `0` to `9` only.

Each root-to-leaf path in the tree represents a number. For example, the root-to-leaf path `1 → 2 → 3` represents the number `123`.

Return the **total sum of all root-to-leaf numbers**. A **leaf** is a node with no children. The answer is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit integer.
questions.title: Sum Root to Leaf Numbers
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 1000]
The depth of the tree will not exceed 10
The answer is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit integer

questions.question:
A binary tree is described by an array `indexes` where the i-th row (1-indexed) gives the indices of node i's left and right children; a value of `-1` means no child. Node 1 is the root and sits at depth 1.

For each query value `k`, **swap the left and right subtrees** of every node whose depth is a multiple of `k` (i.e. depth `k, 2k, 3k, …`). After performing a query's swaps, record the **inorder traversal** of the tree. Swaps from earlier queries persist into later ones.

Return the list of inorder traversals, one per query.
questions.title: Swap Nodes [Algo]
constraints: Node values are the node indices 1..n; the root is node 1 at depth 1

questions.question:
A binary tree is described by an array `indexes` where the i-th row (1-indexed) gives the indices of node i's left and right children; a value of `-1` means no child. Node 1 is the root and sits at **depth 1**.

For each query value `k`, **swap the left and right subtrees** of every node whose depth is a multiple of `k` (i.e. depths `k, 2k, 3k, …`). After performing a query's swaps, record the **inorder traversal** of the tree. Swaps from earlier queries **persist** into later ones.

Return the list of inorder traversals, one per query.
questions.title: Swap Nodes [Algo]
constraints: Node values are the node indices 1..n; the root is node 1 at depth 1

questions.question:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, check whether it is a **mirror of itself** (i.e., symmetric around its center).

A tree is symmetric if the left subtree is a mirror reflection of the right subtree: the structures match and the values match when one side is read left-to-right and the other right-to-left.
questions.title: Symmetric Tree
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 1000]
Follow-up: solve it both recursively and iteratively

questions.question:
You are given a tree with `n` nodes, where node `i` has weight `w[i]`. Choose a subset `S` of nodes maximizing the total weight `Σ w[i]` over `i ∈ S`, subject to the constraint that ***no two chosen nodes are adjacent*** (connected by an edge).

Return the maximum achievable total weight.
questions.title: Maximum Weight Independent Set on a Tree
constraints: Weights w[i] can be any integer (including negatives — skipping a negative node is allowed)
The graph is a tree: n − 1 edges, connected, no cycles
Total weight fits in 64-bit (use long in Java)

questions.question:
The height of a binary tree is the number of **edges** between the tree's root and its furthest leaf.

Given the `root` of a binary tree, return its height.

For example, a tree with a single node has height `0`, because there are no edges below the root.
questions.title: Tree: Height of a Binary Tree
constraints: The tree is non-empty (at least the root exists)
Height is counted in edges, so a single node has height 0

questions.question:
You are given the `root` of a prebuilt **Huffman tree** and an encoded binary string `s`. In the tree, every leaf stores one original character; internal nodes are structural placeholders. The encoding assigns each character the sequence of left/right turns ('0' = left, '1' = right) from the root to its leaf.

**Decode** `s` back into the original string and print it.
questions.title: Tree: Huffman Decoding
constraints: The Huffman tree is already built and valid (prefix-free)
Every leaf holds exactly one character; internal nodes hold a placeholder
'0' means go left, '1' means go right

questions.question: Given a pointer to the `root` of a binary tree, print the **inorder traversal** of the tree: the values visited in Left-subtree, Node, Right-subtree order, separated by spaces.
questions.title: Tree: Inorder Traversal
constraints: Output values are space-separated in inorder sequence

questions.question: Given a pointer to the `root` of a binary tree, print its **level-order traversal**: the node values visited top-to-bottom and, within each level, left-to-right, separated by spaces.
questions.title: Tree: Level Order Traversal
constraints: Output values are space-separated in level-order sequence

questions.question: Given a pointer to the `root` of a binary tree, print the **postorder traversal** of the tree: the values visited in Left-subtree, Right-subtree, Node order, separated by spaces.
questions.title: Tree: Postorder Traversal
constraints: Output values are space-separated in postorder sequence

questions.question: Given a pointer to the `root` of a binary tree, print the **preorder traversal** of the tree: the values visited in Node, Left-subtree, Right-subtree order, separated by spaces.
questions.title: Tree: Preorder Traversal
constraints: Output values are space-separated in preorder sequence

questions.question:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, determine if it is a **valid binary search tree (BST)**.

A valid BST is defined as follows:

- The left subtree of a node contains only nodes with keys **strictly less** than the node's key.
- The right subtree of a node contains only nodes with keys **strictly greater** than the node's key.
- Both the left and right subtrees must also be binary search trees.
questions.title: Validate Binary Search Tree
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 10⁴]
-2³¹ ≤ Node.val ≤ 2³¹ − 1 (values can equal Integer.MIN_VALUE / MAX_VALUE — beware overflow)
Duplicates are not allowed under the strict ordering

questions.question:
Design a data structure that supports adding new words and finding if a string matches any previously added string.

Implement the `WordDictionary` class:

- `WordDictionary()` initializes the object.
- `void addWord(word)` adds `word` to the data structure, it can be matched later.
- `bool search(word)` returns `true` if there is any string in the data structure that matches `word` or `false` otherwise. `word` may contain dots `'.'` where dots can be matched with **any** letter.
questions.title: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
constraints: word in addWord consists of lowercase English letters
word in search consists of '.' or lowercase English letters
There will be at most 2 dots in word for search queries when calling search
At most 10⁴ calls will be made to addWord and search

questions.question:
A **trie** (pronounced *try*) or **prefix tree** is a tree data structure used to efficiently store and retrieve keys in a set of strings. There are various applications of this data structure, such as autocomplete and spellchecker.

Implement the `Trie` class:

- `Trie()` initializes the trie object.
- `void insert(String word)` inserts the string `word` into the trie.
- `boolean search(String word)` returns `true` if `word` is in the trie (i.e. was inserted before), and `false` otherwise.
- `boolean startsWith(String prefix)` returns `true` if there is a previously inserted string `word` that has the prefix `prefix`, and `false` otherwise.
questions.title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
constraints: word and prefix consist only of lowercase English letters
At most 3 × 10⁴ calls in total will be made to insert, search, and startsWith

questions.question:
In English, we have a concept called **root**, which can be followed by some other word to form another longer word — let's call this word a **successor**. For example, when the root `"help"` is followed by the word `"ful"`, we can form a successor `"helpful"`.

Given a `dictionary` consisting of many roots and a `sentence` consisting of words separated by spaces, replace all the successors in the sentence with the **root forming it**. If a successor can be replaced by more than one root, replace it with the root that has the **shortest length**.

Return the sentence after the replacement.
questions.title: Replace Words

examples.input: dictionary = ["cat","bat","rat"], sentence = "the cattle was rattled by the battery"
examples.output: "the cat was rat by the bat"

constraints: dictionary[i] consists of only lowercase letters
sentence consists of only lowercase letters and spaces
The number of words in sentence is in the range [1, 1000]
Every two consecutive words in sentence are separated by exactly one space

questions.question:
Given an `m x n` board of characters and a list of strings `words`, return **all words on the board**.

Each word must be constructed from letters of sequentially adjacent cells, where adjacent cells are horizontally or vertically neighboring. The same letter cell may not be used **more than once** in a word.
questions.title: Word Search II
constraints: board[i][j] is a lowercase English letter
All strings in words are unique
